article: Fifty years later. I am sitting in a helicopter flying low over the frozen wastelands, assault rifle in my hands, feeling nervous. My comrades are talking quietly; Korzhev and Tatarov are playing dice. Lukashenko, we all call him just Luka, is handing round a flask of vodka. I glance up to see if Sergeant Miskalov is watching before I accept it. It goes down warm and helps to soothe my nerves as I sit by the open doorway watching the endless pine forests pass by. We land and the five of us drag our gear out of the chopper before it lifts away and is gone again. We are here, in the middle of nowhere, and it's as cold as hell. A short trek across the frozen landscape takes us to the old base. We've studied plans and satellite imaging already before leaving Kansk, but still, we don't know what to expect when we get inside. The buildings, all heavily reinforced concrete, are still intact despite fifty years abandonment. Miskalov orders us to stop at the perimeter fence and I scan the site, first with binoculars, then with infra red sensors and geiger counter. Nothing. There are a few signs of the life that was here, back in 65. Military vehicles, decayed by time and the elements, stand where they were left all that time ago. Luka stands next to me. "What do you think, Dobry?" I pack up the equipment and pick up my rifle again. "Nothing here," I say with a faked smile as I slap him on the shoulder. "We'll be back in Kansk before suppertime." They told us that they don't know what happened here, but I reckon they do. Rumours and conspiracy theories abound of course, some say it was an alien from a crashed UFO, some say it was a yeti, most of us think it was some secret Soviet experiment that went badly wrong. Whatever it was, I just hope it's not still here. Miskalov orders us to move in and we do just that, Korzhev leading the way as usual, like the mad bastard he is. The first thing that hits us as we step inside the first building is the smell, like the inside of a grave. And it soon becomes apparent, once we get our lights on, that's exactly what it is. There are bodies everywhere, all badly decayed, some piled up by the door as though they were trying to escape. Some are broken; limbs torn off, torsos ripped in half. I gag and try not to spew my breakfast over the floor. We move through the facility silently, through room after room, each one a silent frozen grave. "Did you hear that?" Tatarov whispers. "Hear what?" says Luka. "The only thing I hear is your fat mouth," Korzhev replies, giving Tatarov a shove with the butt of his rifle. "That and your incessant farting, but I can't always tell the difference." "Fuck you," Tatarov mutters. I don't say anything. I heard it too but it was just wolves out in the forest. We come to a door marked "Tunguska Research" and we glance at each other. "Tunguska?" I say aloud, exchanging a glance with Miskalov. "That was like, over a hundred years ago." Everyone in Russia knows about Tunguska, the meteor strike that flattened the forest a couple of hundred miles west of where we are. Sarge shrugs and opens the door. The room is large and there are fewer bodies in here so the smell isn't so bad. It's kitted out like an old fashioned medical facility. There are hospital beds, some still occupied by the corpses of the men that died in them. The extreme cold dry air has almost mummified them. I go over to one of the beds to inspect a body. The skin is stretched tight over the skeleton, the face in a permanent grin. Odd looking fellow, his teeth are almost pointed, with pronounced canines. "Hey Dobry, look at this," Luka calls to me from the far end of the room. The wall is stacked high with cages, thirty or more of them and in each one, the remains of a dead animal. Dogs maybe, or wolves. "Looks like they were experimenting on the local wildlife," I say to him. The poor things must have just starved to death after whatever happened to the people who fed them. I glance back at the corpse on the bed and get an uneasy feeling in the pit of my stomach. Miskalov is pulling out the contents of every filing cabinet he can find, putting the files into packs to take back for further study. I head over to join him but we're all alerted by a yell from Korzhev. "What the fuck!" He's standing by what looks like an autopsy table and on it is another corpse, but like nothing I've ever seen in my life before. Even though it's mummified like the others, it's huge. Well over seven feet tall, and must have been an enormous beast when it was alive. For beast it is, not human, despite the humanoid shape. It has the skull of a wolf and the body is still covered in thick fur. "Let's get out of here," Tatarov says with a trembling voice. For once, Sarge agrees with him and we head out back the way we came. The noise comes again as he's about to radio for the chopper. Howling, like wolves, close. Very close. I raise my rifle and fire. - On a desk in an office at Kansk Airbase, five files are closed. Sergeant Boris Miskalov. Private Piotr Korzhev. Private Dmitri Lukashenko. Private Ivan Tatarov. Private Aleksandr Dobrykin. Missing, presumed dead.

article: To be completely honest, I never thought I would see this day come. Sure, crazy people on the corner of city streets would constantly preach about it day in and day out. And yeah, I heard the news stories lately about the rapidly degrading conditions of Earth. But c'mon. If someone told me yesterday that the world was 100 going to end, I would have told them that they were a silly goose who hadn't yet stepped outside to see what a beautiful day it was. That's what really threw me off. It was an absolutely gorgeous day yesterday! The sun was shining, not a cloud in sight. The Earth smelled green and new. Today was no exception. It was a normal Spring day. I woke up at my normal morning time 9 AM. I poured myself my normal cup of joe in my normal "I Heart Pugs" mug. Everything was so..... normal! It wasn't until a giant crack split my neighbor's house in half that I realized anything was wrong. To be honest though, Bobby was planning on moving out within the month anyway. It wasn't like he was in it when it happened. Thank God! Gee, that would have been truly disastrous. Anyway, so everyone began screaming in the streets. The sun was still shining above. Not a cloud in sight. The weather was breezy and beautiful as ever. The cracks in the ground were pretty darn deep, but then again we live in California. We should be used to earthquakes, right? Well I got ta admit, it was a bit excessive. So I grabbed up my little dachshund, Scoobs, and packed up my car with only the necessities since we were in a bit of a rush. I zoomed on down the street. I had offered Barbara a ride when I passed her house, but she was too frantic. I hadn't seen her this frazzled since the Black Friday Target fiasco of 2005. I continued on my way down to my favorite bar. I checked in to see if Lou was alright. He was pretty crazed too. The TV was ranting about all of this insanity being the Apocalypse or something. I didn't really pay it too much mind. I tried to calm a very distraught, sobbing Lou. He refused to move from behind the bar. I sighed and decided it best to keep on driving. If this truly was the "End of Time," then I thought it would be nice to take a scenic route so I can pass by the beaches. It would've been such a shame to pass up the opportunity considering it was such a beautiful day. I called my family members while driving. All of them were hysterical. I reassured them that even if this was the end, we all loved each other and that's all that really matters. Plus, we got to go on a wonderful family cruise last summer that visited the European countries of Greece, Italy, and Turkey. I very much believe that it healed our family in a lot of ways. Knowing that we have those precious memories makes up for not being together right now. Oh my, I better finish writing this little entry. You see, I've been an optimist about this whole ordeal. I've really believed that this would all pass. However, there is a quite terrifying tsunami headed my way as I type this. Not to mention, I passed many a house on fire and a few out of place tornadoes. My drive yesterday eventually led me here, a secluded beach somewhere in Northern California. I found a little shack and decided to write a little bit before kicking the bucket. Now although my optimism may be frowned upon by some possibly many, I must let you the reader understand that I was never completely shielded from reality. I knew there was a good chance that this really was the end. I only kept my hope alive because it would ensure, perhaps, a happier and more tranquil death. I am no fool. Death is an inevitable part of life. I am just content that I got to drive down this gorgeous Californian coast on a beautiful Spring day, got to call my family and tell them I love them, and got to find this quaint beach the last place I will ever visit. Here I have spent my last moments documenting my experience in the last 24 hours with a view like no other and my dog by my side. The wave is quite high now. Wow. Look at it! Must be a thousand stories high! Slightly sad now that I couldn't be on the coast of Hawaii or some other island. The water would have probably been a lot bluer and clearer! Oh well. You win some and you lose some. Ah! So my optimism remains! Even with this impressive wave about to consume me and Scoobs. A wise man by the name of Plato once said, "We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark; the real tragedy of life is when men are afraid of the light." I can't say for sure Plato is talking about the afterlife. I was never the smartest cookie in the cookie jar. However for the purpose of my tale, I believe that is indeed what he is talking about. My optimism has allowed me to reject this idea of fear. I am excited for the light. I welcome it. In my head, I am waving farewell to you reader with the tune "Goodbye Stranger" playing in the background. Real cinematic like. I'll see you on the flip side, friend.

It can help them overcome their phobia by teaching them that the object or situation is not as dangerous as they initially believed. Additionally, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) has also been found to be effective for treating specific phobias.

So we crave them because of our evolutionary history, and now that we can have as much as we want, we have a tendency to abuse the situation.','There are no good foods or bad foods. You could theoretically spark when unplugging (low probability) or when going from grounded to undgrounded back to grounded. (higher probability, but still low). article: Every part of the US federal government (and the CIA is a part of that government) is subjected to 3 forms of oversight: 1: The Congress funds it. Even if it were true (and I doubt) that the CIA has access to funds outside of Congressional supervision, such funds would be a tiny, tiny part of its operating budget and aren't being used to fund anything other than very small, very covert operations.} 2: The President directs it. All the various agencies and departments of the US government work at the direction of the President. Their leadership are all appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate and they serve at the President's discretion. The CIA was created in the mid 1940s when the War Department was reorganized after WWII. Originally the Director of the CIA was a cabinet-level official who reported directly to the President. Today there's a level of bureaucracy in the middle, the Director of National Intelligence (a post created after 911 as a result of the 911 Commission's recommendations) but the head of the CIA still serves at the pleasure of the President. 3: The court system oversees it. The CIA must follow US law and if it does not follow the law the people who broke the law can be and are prosecuted. In addition, in the 1970s a special court was set up, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) court which reviews matters related to intelligence operations within the United States or targeting US persons. All these layers and checks balances are one reason the thunderous bloviation from the Congress about these matters rarely translates into any action. article: Clearly, X is better than Y, for a number of reasons. 1. Pronunciation. Saying X has a stronger, more powerful sound than saying Y, which only manages to sound a bit whiny, perhaps because is is too close to "why." 2. Exclusivity. Only about 300 words in English start with X. Y starts over 700 (per Wolfram-Alpha, and this appears to include proper nouns). X appears in only 0.15 of English words, while Y appears in far more. I could not find an estimated percentage, but so many adverbs end in "ly" that it rather proves my point. Even though it's so exclusive, it is so much more versatile, as shown below. 3. Consistency. X is always a consonant. Y? Well, it cannot make up its mind. 4. Scrabble. X is worth twice as many points (8:4). 5. Use in math. First, x is almost always the first letter used as you learn algebra. This could go with consistency above as well, but the x-axis shows the constant, stable variable. 6. Appearance. X has a strong, stable stance. Y looks like it could topple over in a slight breeze. 7. Sex. Our favorite word not only has X right in it, but the whole last 23 of the word sounds like saying X. Y? Nowhere to be found, unless it tags along to make something sexy. Not to mention the uses of XXX, and the fact that fairer sex is made up of X chromosomes. Y gives us baldness, hairy backs, and emotional immaturity. 8. History. Malcolm X, not Malcolm Y. There's even "American History X." 9. Versatility in other areas. X can be used to show that something is crossed out, used as a check mark to indicate the choice on a form, used in cartoons to show that a person is dead, used in medicine (x-rays), used to show treasure on a map, 10. X. 11. No one has ever died in a state spelled with an X. Kentucky, New Jersey, New York, and Wyoming combine for 10 of the deaths in the US each year I somehow came up with the 4 Y states off the top of my head and also thought there were no X states. New Mexico and Texas. 12. If you're talking about unknown items, you always say "X is better than Y," never "Y is better than X." EDIT: It worked. I was forced to rethink some of my strongest points. article: The songs start when you turn eighteen. You are supposed to hear the voice of your true love. Instead I only heard screeching. It was a sad, broken, and toneless baritone voice. When others asked I would tell them I heard a wonderful voice, but it was too far away. Honestly, it wasn't too far, but it wasn't all that close. My fear and embarrassment kept me away. Years had passed and I was now twenty-four. Today, the screeching became very loud and abruptly stopped. This pattern repeated for the rest of the day. Finally, I couldn't take it anymore. I had to know. I got in my car and followed the voice. It grew louder and louder and finally I was at a hospital. I explained to the nurse at the front desk my problem, but she only told me to leave. I was losing my patience and decided to do something undoubtably stupid. I ran past the nurse and up the stairs. I followed the voice and was met with a white door. I swung it open to see a man lying in bed. His eyes were closed and his blond hair stuck to his sweaty forehead. He was hooked up to at least four machines. I gently and nervously walked forward. The voice pounded in my head. I heard running footsteps behind me. Security had obviously been called. Something compelled me forward and I gripped his hand tightly in my own. One machine made a sound and his hand tightened slightly around my own. Instantly the singing felt peaceful and the eyes of this man opened to reveal a tired chocolate brown. The nurse behind me gasped, and I stiffened as security grabbed me. She then ordered them to let me go and leave the room. "Thomas has been on life support for just over six years. He has been on the brink of death a few times and never woken until now" she informed me as she checked his vitals.'Thomas, so that's his name.' I thought to myself. I felt ashamed. How could I have waited this long to come to him? If I had come sooner would he have been awake sooner? All my fear and anger at myself vanished when he smiled at me. He didn't blame me? We talked the whole next day and I came day after day when I was done with work. He had to stay in the hospital a few more weeks and after that had to undergo physical therapy to walk again. This was hindered more by the fact he had prosthetic legs. He was in the military and was blown up by a land mine while evacuating villagers. He lost both his legs, some of his friends, and his life that he knew all in one day. Now he could have a new chance. When I asked him if he would take that life with me and he said yes I was greatful. I didn't deserve such a great man, but I was there every day. The voice gradually changed to a happy and mildly broken tone. Then evened out to be pure joy; although still toneless I found it beautiful. I don't know why it was different on that day, but sometimes I wish the voice had urged me forward sooner. I'm not sure why I ran past the desk and to his room or why I touched Thomas. I guess love just makes you do crazy things and I'm thankful for it.

article: Death in God's harem was quick and commonplace. My life had been flipped upside down since I was taken several years ago. I don't know what they were, demons, spirits, or aliens. All I know is they ruled our world from the shadows. They were brutal and instigated most of our problems, stomping on anyone who achieved too much, or stepped too close to the truth. I was taken for my artistic abilities, others for their intelligence, charisma, or strength. One thing was common however. Male or female, we were all beautiful. The creature that owned us called itself God, a word it used to mock the faith of those who believed. I felt a bright light fill my vision. Instinctively I closed my eyes, to no avail. The light invaded anything and just as suddenly, it left. 22, the number floated above my head. It represented God's favor, how much he enjoyed us. Thousands lived inside this sprawling underground complex, and their power and position was decided from the whim of a volatile invader. My number had been 24 just moments ago. Two people had lost God's favor, and their lives. The numbers represented our hierarchy in this world. Single digits were given vast amounts of power. They lived comfortable pampered lives, and could toy with the others as they would. They could even request for new acquisitions. It was said that God allowed 1 a single wish, within reasonable boundaries. " 22, come here. " A voice pierced the darkness of my studio. A young Norwegian woman stepped from behind a curtain, and pulled off her headdress revealing a bright twinkling 3 where a 5 had been just a day before. " Now that I'm 3rd, I'm entitled to suites and servants to keep them. You're my maid now. " 3 walked up to me, slowly. She wore a red and black silk dress that shifted as she walked, emphasizing her perfect body. I bit my lip to quench my anxiety, and looked at her long booted legs. She had been captured on the same day as me and given numbers in the thousands, yet she had risen so incredibly fast. We had been lovers outside, but the harem had changed her. She had grown cold, distant, worshipping God wholeheartedly. She had turned cruel, plotting and hurting any she could. She had grown to hate our former relationship, or at least had grown to love beating and humiliating me. " As you wish, 3, " I said as I lowered my head. " Look me in the eye, " she ordered as she placed a hand on my cheek and lifted my face. Her cold blue eyes sliced into mine, beautiful yet emotionless. For a second I felt her eyes flash, and the old warmth seep through. Then her face softened as she smiled the same dazzling smile I remembered as my heart leaped out of my chest. " Jessica. Don't worry. Once I get to First..., " and then the warmth was gone. She raised her left hand and slapped my face hard before pushing me away and scattering my artworks over the studio floor. Days of work, ruined. I was to present them for God's celebration at the end of the week. I sobbed as I collapsed on the floor. " Do you know why 3 and 4 were killed? " 3 asked me as she walked toward the door. " No, 3rd why? " I gasped out. " They loved each other more than God. "

article: Alicia, now she was a real piece of work. Said she didn't feel good. Sat there sulking at our meeting. We were supposed to be discussing the next step on our research assignment on the cardiovascular effects of diabetes on women over 50 but she sat there, quiet, staring at her phone. So I poked, I proded, trying to get her to talk. I mean, if she was just another coworker I wouldn't care, but we were sort of friends at this point. She had a way of trapping you in a friendship. But yeah, finally she responded with, "I was assaulted." And then back to silently staring at her phone. If that were her excuse for not having her work done, and not being prepared for this meeting, it was pretty messed up. But I gave her the benefit of the doubt. I poked some more, she refused to answer. "People say I'm beautiful. I hear that at least five times a day. It's amazing." She said that as she admired herself in her phone-mirror. I had no response to that, so I suggested ending the meeting and reconvening at another, more convenient, time. "Sure, leave me, that's what I deserve." At this point I started to get pretty annoyed. Do you want to talk, then, I ask. "You're a man, you won't understand." I didn't even know what to say to that. I wanted to say, okay don't talk to me, then. Or I wanted to just get my things and leave. But as infuriating as she was, I also felt bad for her. Or she made me feel bad for her. I mean, she had just said she was assaulted. So I decided to stick around and ask her again what happened, even though I didn't care and wouldn't understand. Finally, she relented. Or this was just the next move in the game she was playing. She finally looked up from her phone, tears in her eyes. "You know the support group I run for discrminated youth at the student union? This man came in and yelled at us and told us we were wasting everyone's time! He was so rude and obnoxious. And obviously he walks away without any consequences." I was confused, and it showed in my expression. "Well, you could say I was verbally assaulted," she said. I swept up my things and walked out.

article: First, we need to look at each topic- honor and family- separately: East Asian cultures tend to place a high value on the concept of honor (Asian cultures aren't alone in this, but it is particularly emphasized in East Asian cultures). Honor is tied to a person's reputation, the image they present to the world, and the respect they receive from others. In East Asian cultures, honor is related to one's family and social status. Similarly, family is also given great importance in East Asian cultures. Family loyalty is considered fundamental, and the hierarchical structure of the family is emphasized. The eldest members of the family, particularly the father or grandfather, are often given great respect and authority. Both honor and family are linked in East Asian cultures. Maintaining one's family honor is considered a duty, and family members are expected to uphold the honor of the family. This means that the actions of one family member can reflect poorly on the entire family. Therefore, family members are often expected to make sacrifices for the sake of the family's honor and reputation. Overall, honor and family are deeply intertwined in East Asian cultures. Family members are expected to maintain the honor and reputation of the family, and this is linked to the importance placed on a person's social status and image in society.

article: This will probably get buried as I'm late to the party, but couldn't resist - the prompt is too good! This isn't that horrifying either, I just came up with it in traffic and kind of went with it. Good practice I guess. Bank station. The busiest on the network, nearly a hundred thousand passengers each morning travel through here, arriving to make their daily trudge through the city of London to their jobs. Most of them work in banking. They're easy to spot, with suits from Saville Row, shirts from Jermyn Street, and morals darker than the deepest recesses of Soho. Profiling a target is a doddle, and the execution comes naturally. Growing up on the estate, I was never going to be allowed into the rarefied air of the Bank of England or Lloyds of London. Once Mum had her benefits cut, I had to pay my way, it's not uncommon. Lads on BMX bikes move weed and whatever else they can get their hands on, but I was never tough enough to look after myself in those gangs. I ended up shoplifting, a quick stroll over to Oxford Circus, snip off the tags and tailgate a tourist out. Easy. Too easy. There's no skill to shoplifting, not like pickpocketing. I had a good teacher, a modern day Fagin if you will, though the flat caps of Oliver Twist were replaced by snapbacks, tags still attached of course. After a few years I went solo, still staying in touch with my old mates to make I wasn't stepping on anyone's toes. You rarely get a nicely worded letter from these boys if you're on their patch. Bank is so busy I can act with impunity, plenty of bankers for everyone. This one was perfect. I saw him run through the barriers, flustered, late, fumbling with his oyster card. He carefully checked his wallet before throwing the card in there, a flash of blue still visible as he slid it into his inside jacket pocket. This was almost too easy. I moved towards the door where he was stood, ostensibly to pick up a discarded copy of the Metro from a seatback. I didn't feel like reading, but it looks natural, and a freesheet is a bloody good prop, even if it is plastered in the latest story of debauched footballers. He was lost in his own world, checking his phone every five seconds, looking for the red blinking LED that has enslaved so many in this city. Even easier. He goes for the door, I watch his shoulders, tailing him through the barriers as he taps the wallet on the reader. He's going left, towards the exit for the Bank. I feint left and go right, my shoulder crashing into his chest. A flutter of newsprint and a thousand tuts from the commuters and I'm home and dry, the soft leather wallet nestling in my jacket now. I cross the platforms and jump on a tube heading east, time for a spot of lunch and a bit more work. Westfield Stratford, a hell of a shopping centre, and close enough to home to know shorten my commute back. I'm in need of a new t-shirt and I guess old habits die hard. Maybe a quick lift to top up the beer kitty for tonight. Quick scan and boom. A yank, can spot them from a mile off. They always dress like they're going into battle, rucksacks, sunnies, hat, bottles of water, as if anywhere outside of the USofA lacks even basic amenities. Not that I'm complaining, all those pockets make theft a doddle. I stroll past to get a look at the bag, but before I can she turns, and I freeze. "Hey, can you help me?" I was right, definitely American. Right, new tack. The accent goes on, no more wide boy charm, time for the full Cumberbatch.'I certainly hope so my dear, how can I be of service to you?' She smiles sweetly, and asks for some advice. Don't hang around with reprobates like me would be a good start, luv. Keep it moving "Let's walk and talk, it's a big place and we won't see it all from standing still." I introduce her to a few shops, she's in London for 2 days before her friends fly in. "Well it's a terrible shame for a lovely lady like you to be all alone. I wouldn't be much of a gentleman if I didn't offer to keep you company for a while. Fancy a spot of lunch?" She's in. Wahaca. Chelada. Tostada. We chat, it beats eating lunch alone. She's tidy, decent chassis on her in a pair of shorts and a hollister tee. Long blonde hair and a tendency to use'like' as punctuation, I'd guessed she was from California long before she divulged that fact. Whether it was the light glinting off her straw coloured locks, or the refraction of it through the amber beer, I felt good. I pay for lunch and take my leave, demanding only a hug as payment for her company. As we embrace I slide fifty quid out of her unguarded pocket, which covers lunch and my time. Off home, stopping on the way to pick up a henry and some king size rizla for the evening ahead. Through the door, trainers off and jacket over the chair, time for a brew. Fucking hell, I almost forgot, that wallet I took this morning. Chatting to that American bird distracted me more than I thought. Good job I wrote my number on the back of a tube ticket for her. I try not to bring evidence home if I can help it. Wallets get stripped of the good stuff and binned, phones are fenced down the local before I get home, the more unusual stuff I take a view on. Let's take a look at the wallet. It's nicer than I thought. Hand stitched, the leather is softer than I've ever felt before. The tip of the oyster card still peeks out from it. Two hundred bats cash. Nice. American Express Platinum, standard, and a nice way to assuage my guilt. Anyone with one of these can afford to lose a few bob. Few more bits and bobs. Mostly crap. Still, no stone unturned and all that. There's a slip of paper tucked inside, folded carefully. It's a photo. Who even carries photos any more? A photo of a baby in an incubator. Shit. That's what he was looking at. On the phone. He wasn't waiting for notification, he was looking at the wallpaper, the very same photo. Fuck it, he's got a digital copy of it then, nothing fifty pence at Boots can't solve for a reprint. There's more paper on the other side of the pocket, but it doesn't look like cash, I take a quick look so I can bin what I don't need on the way to the pub. Order of Service. Oh Christ. She was called Molly. He buried her yesterday. Poor Bastard. His driving licence is still in the wallet. I have to send this back. It's not fair. This is never what I set out to do. The address goes on the envelope, I'll throw it in the post box tomorrow somewhere in the city. Not popping evidence in the box at the bottom of the tower. For now, let's work on this henry. - I'm at Oxford Circus today, I don't want to go back to Bank in case I see him again. I'm not afraid, just ashamed. The letter goes in the postbox, swallowing at least some of my guilt in its wide red mouth as well. Time to go to work. Same routine, I take a seat and wait for some idiot tourist to advertise themselves. Another yank dressed like they're off to battle Rommel jumps on, and I grab my prop. No footballer today though. Seems some banker decided to take the quickest route from the top of the walkie talkie to the slabs below. I've seen that name before. Not half an hour ago as I dropped it through the slot.

article: Two main processes were highlighted in the Microbiology book I have (Bauman, 2006). The first one consists of four basic steps, and the goal is to remove toxins and microorganisms which cause disease. One of the big steps in removing aerobic microorganisms is removing their oxygen source, which prevents them from breaking down nutrients. 1. Primary treatment - Wastewater is pumped into large tanks where it's allowed to settle. Lightweight solids, grease, and floating particles are skimmed off the top, and heavier materials settle on the bottom into sludge. A flocculating agent, alum, is added, which basically makes particles clump together and sink to the bottom of the tank to join the sludge. The sludge is then removed, and the water moves on to further treatment. 2. Secondary treatment - Basically, the water is aerated to facilitate the growth of microbes which will remove dissolved organic materials by metabolizing them into carbon dioxide or water. In the activated sludge system, the water is basically pumped into a sludgy mixture, where the microbes in the sludge start digesting what's left in the water. The water is then moved to an oxygen-free environment, and the sludge does its magic, removing oxygen, "starving" the remaining microbes. Smaller communities sometimes pass it through a sand filter in this step, but it's less effective. 3. Chemical treatment. The water is treated somehow, usually with chlorine, sometimes with UV or ozone. It's then either released into rivers or the ocean, or used to irrigate crops and highway vegetation. 4. Sludge treatment. More microbes are used to break down the sludge into carbon dioxide and other organic materials. The second system is artificial wetlands, which are pretty neat but require a much larger area. Essentially, the water is passed through a series of artificially-constructed ponds where the natural microbiota gradually break down the sediments and wastes. It's then treated (sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection via UV, chlorine, or ozone) and released back into the water supply. Hope this helps!','1. Water is collected in a single big deposit, like an artificial lake, or a tank. 2. Screening: This is when they remove large waste, mainly plastic and other things that don't dissolve in water, including bags, cotton, rags.... etc. This is pretty much like putting water through a sieve. 3. Primary Treatment: This is when they remove solid matter, in other words, poop. We're not worried about making the water drinkable yet, we just want to get the bulk of the waste out. This is done by putting the water into large tanks and literally letting it sit until all the solid sinks to the bottom. 4. Secondary treatment: The water now doesn't have any visible bits of solid, but it's still very filthy. This step is to remove smaller things out of the water, including insects and eggs. The water is put into active lanes and we pump air through the water (Bubbling) to encourage "good bacteria" growth. This bacteria will essentially killreduce 'bad bacteria'. 5. Tertiary treatment: The good bacteria has done it's job and now it needs to go as well. The water is placed back into another tank where it's allowed to settle. The bacteria sinks to the bottom and is removed like sludge from the bottom of the tank. 6. Sludge treatment: The process creates a large amount of waste (Mainly poop and bacteria) which is normally sludgy. The sludge is normally shipped off and either incinerated, or in some placed it gets pumped to gas recycling stations because it can generate a large amount of methane to be used as fuel.

article: If we want to actually be non-discriminatory, race, religion, gender, and sexual orientation should not be included in college applications or considered during admission reviews. A thread called rWritingPrompts is not helping writers sat at the top, the most upvoted by far. That said enough. Oh, he'd tried to delete his comment. But once you reach a certain level of notoriety, that only makes things worse. People post screenshots. There was no end to the mockery. There was no turning back. Another red envelope. He clicked without even thinking. "Kill yourself." That was not the first time he'd heard such a thing. In school, he'd been bullied by a girl for committing the heinous crime of asking her out. After that, she never left him alone. She had a talent for drawing, and a sick mind. She'd leave him presents in his school bag - drawings of an erotic nature, but not the kind a 15 year old boy would hope for. She'd also show these drawings to her friends, and the rest of the class, for that matter. No one ever looked at him the same way again. That's how talented she was. Oh, he dabbled in drawing too. In fact, he had always harbored naive dreams of becoming an animator for Disney. One of the reasons why he had fallen for this girl was that he greatly admired her talent. One day, in class, she snatched a doodle from his hands. What ensued was unbearable. She'd show it to everyone and explain to everyone why it sucked, and why she was so much better than him, and he'd never amount to anything. In fact, no explanation was necessary. That was the worst part. It was obvious he was a hack. Torture followed him around for the remainder of high school. After graduation, he did pre-med, then med school. There wasn't an artistic bone left in his body - she had made sure of that. He was just glad that people didn't bully him anymore. They mostly just ignored him, bar an acquaintance or two. But the farther he got in med school, the lonelier he became. And one day, he realized that the only reason he had chosen medicine was because it seemed the reasonable choice at the time. He had truly fled from his dream. He couldn't draw anymore. Too painful. So he took to writing short fiction. Of course, he'd beat himself up for how awful his stories were. Often, weeks went by without him getting a single word down. But then he stumbled upon rWritingPrompts. He didn't even remember the first prompt he'd responded to. Something stupid like Batman invents fedoras that kill people. Oddjob challenges him to a duel. He'd typed up a quick response, and one or two people actually upvoted him. That was validation enough to keep writing. And surely enough, he became more and more confident and productive. article: When you enter into a contract, the expectation is that the terms are to remain consistent. Although there may be provisions for what happens when someone violates the contract, simply changing them without notice is ridiculous. I admit recently contracts have began to change while in place, but this is only recently and as a result of increased reliance on the concept of intellectual property, and it's still a fairly murky issue anyway. The issue I have with mandatory national service is that, assuming the government is a "social contract," it by nature is a "shifting of the terms." When you're in service, what's expected of you is obviously different than when you're not in service. I may completely disagree or object to serving under a military code of conduct, or whatever it may be. I'd also argue that the "social contract" should be given MORE scrutiny as to its extent than a normal contract. You have to typically reach the age of majority to make contracts of any validity, and typically have options to not make a given contract due to the nature of private competition between businesses and persons, or certain things not being necessary. When things are a monopoly, or difficult to not have, there's regulations so as to ensure bargaining power isn't completely out of hand. The "social contract" is in place since one's birth, non-optional, and very difficult to find a different alternative given immigration laws, and non-liquid capital. Given that it's a bit of a stretch of the terms of a contract already, I don't think it would help to give it even more elbow room. Quite simply. if a government can make its entire body directly work for them against their own wishes, it can do anything, and I feel that power could easily be abused. Of course the draft should be instituted in certain cases where the nation's being directly invaded, but I don't think such places could ever apply in the modern era. It certainly wasn't justified any time it was used in the past; forcing people to serve in the Civil War, even though it was valid, sets precedent for forcing people to serve a country being justly rebelled against, and every other time the draft was used the US wasn't being directly attacked, with the exception of WW2, where the front very quickly drew away from US territories. I feel as if the draft should have been dropped when that happened. In the modern era, if the US was invaded, it would either be by a major power (in which case nuclear options would be in consideration) or by small decentralized clusters (which an army without training would be very little help against). Either way, the draft would be a bit useless. Yes, it could produce positive results, but I don't feel as if the possibility to produce those results is worth giving the government so much extra authority.

article: I bought this one avocado a year and a half ago. I was just making guacamole, it was a pretty ordinary experience really. I had about four of them and as I was preparing them. I decided to eat a slice of one. It was a blessing at that time, because if I had never eaten a slice from that particular avocado, I never would have known what a legend of an avocado I had purchased. The flavor, the texture, everything about was unlike anything I imagined could actually exist in the world. I hastily ate another slice from the avocado, and all too quickly that one was gone. I could do what my body was telling me and eat the rest of this unbelievable avocado, but I needed to save it. To eat it all at once would be a waste, and the rest of my life would be a never ending desire for that avocado. So, I wrapped it and put it in my fridge. I began working on the guacamole again, but I only got halfway through before I started worrying what would happen to the new-found purpose of my life that was now wrapped up and in the fridge. I grabbed my half-finished guacamole, pulled everything out of the fridge and got in so I could watch the avocado to make sure it was alright. I was hungry after a while and I tried to eat my half eaten guacamole, but after the first bite I couldn't bring myself to try again. It was truly depressing how the guacamole tasted, there was nothing enjoyable about it at all. The terrible aftertaste of inferior avocados hung around in mouth before I caved in and took another bite from the perfect avocado. But time had taken it's toll, and it didn't bring about the same feelings..... what a waste I had made of something so great. Crying, I ate what little magic remained of the once great avocado. Try to understand, it was still very good, but it wasn't the same. I had made a poor choice. I tried to keep my life the same as it always was, but after a week of holding back, I couldn't do it anymore. I quit my job. Over the next few months, I spent most of my savings sampling avocados. I would buy them from the store, three at a time. I would eat them right at the register, and spit them all out because there wasn't anything remotely enjoyable about them. They didn't even come close. With what little money I had, I started growing my own avocados. I have to sell most of them to keep myself alive. It's hard to resist trying them all, even though the only bring disappointment. The consistent worry that I've sold another perfect avocado to someone else often keeps me awake at night. I have my phone number on all of the avocados and I tell everyone to call if they experience a truly amazing avocado. I get about one call a week, but I can tell just by listening to their voice that they haven't experienced an truly perfect avocado, only one that's better than the rest. Just in case I someone does discover an avocado that is truly as great as the one I found that fateful April, every avocado I grow is gets a number. I take a picture of every avocado so I know the tree it came from, and the location on that tree. I take a picture of every avocado so if I find a truly enjoyable avocado again, I can know the date it was picked and the weather conditions that lead up to it. It feels hopeless and it's a lot of work for no reward as of yet, but I can take no chances. I have to find another perfect avocado. I have to have them consistently. Only then will I be able to experience happiness again.

article: 4:00 AM: Wake up it's a good thing you've never slept that much anyway. The leader of the free world isn't entitled to 40 winks. 20 if you're lucky and that's on a slow day. But today is the inauguration. You weren't really asleep, anyway. 4:30 AM: You're all dressed and briefed on your day's itinerary. Your speechwriters are going over some final revisions while you sip a coffee, straight black. The first hints of sunlight are drawing spikes on the DC skyline. It's going to be a cold, beautiful day. 5:00 AM: Breakfast with the wife and incoming cabinet. Smiles and jokes for the 24 hour news to eat up. 6:00 AM: Worship services at the First Presbyterian Church. More photo-ops for the news. You go over your speech in your head while you appear to pray. And other things. 7:00 AM: You depart for the capitol. In the grand tradition of American democracy, the mantle of power is passing on to you by the will of the people. It warms the cockles of your heart almost as much as your millions do. You ride along with the old guy a gesture symbolizing this grand tradition. He doesn't say much, and spends the ride staring out the window. Up close you can see he has some scars on his face covered with makeup. 8:00 AM: The festivities are in full swing. The US poet laureate, whom you have never nor will ever personally meet, and whose name you will have forgotten an hour from now, is reading an interminable poem about America's beauty for the crowd of thousands assembled on the mall. You are in the wings, discussing the last-last-minute details of your speech. The old guy is nowhere to be seen; he'll appear on stage with the other dignitaries, another old tradition. 9:00 AM: Showtime. You stroll out onto the stage, all swagger and cocksure. The podium is decked in patriotic bunting and balloons. The crowd below is wailing with almost religious fervor. You can see your breath and your cheeks are stinging, but despite the cold you take off your black gloves to wave. You are resplendent. 9:45 AM: Your speech draws to a close. Wild applause. The pundits are already saying that your performance has surprised and that you are an unexpectedly eloquent statesman. At least according to the aides chattering in your earpiece. The old guy is among the many lining up to shake your hand, before he returns to the White House and a helicopter ride aboard Marine One destined for his home in Chi-town. You notice that the Canadian Prime Minister is missing he was there for your speech, but he seems to have disappeared into thin air. 11:00 AM: You complete the arduous walk from the Capitol to the White House. Surrounded by a motorcade and waving to the lookie-loos behind the barricades on both sides of the street, this stroll down Pennsylvania Avenue in the blistering cold has quickly soured you on the many grand traditions surrounding inauguration. 11:30 AM: A final briefing with the old guy in the Oval Office before he screws off forever and leaves you to the business of cleaning up his mess. He hands you a letter: a letter written personally by him, addressed personally to you, which no one else on the planet will ever read. article: Zircon naturally concentrates Uranium in its crystal lattice. Uranium is one of numerous elements which has unstable isotopes. The rate of decay of these isotopes can be used to find out how old something is; while uranium is trapped int he lattice, the daughter isotopes - the things uranium decays to - are not. That means that any of those elements found in the crystal later on are there due to radioactive decay, so you can look at the amount of daughter isotope and calculate the amount of parent that was originally there. If you know the rate that decay happens, then you know the age of the rock. So if you separate the zircons out of a rock you can find the age that those zircon crystals are - how long ago they formed. The only complication here is that zircon is quite a resilient mineral, and it is only formed in igneous rocks. However, if those rocks are eroded then those zircon crystals can end up in later sedimentary rocks. So if you date those zircons you will not get the age of the sedimentary rock, but the older igneous rock the zircon formed in. These "detrital" zircons can be really useful in finding out where sediment has come from to form a particular sedimentary basin.

article: Photo sensitive papers and films are made using a form of silver. The silver halides have a very low activation threshold, and the zap of a photon is enough to knock pieces off the halide, changing it's chemical structure. The film is made by using a substrate which is anything you use to hold the image. It could be plastic, paper, cellulose, etc. The base substrate is embedded with the silver halides and these impregnate the film or paper. It is then dried and packaged in light proof containers. The image is developed using a developer compound like D76, which is a powder dissolved into water to form a liquid developer. It darkens or tarnishes the exposed silver particles. The reaction will keep going until a chemical neutralizer called stopbath is used. Stopbath reacts with the developer and neutralizes it so it stops developing. Without it, an image would continue to get darker and darker over time as the developer continued to work long after it was in a darkroom. Finally the film or paper is run through a chemical called a fixer. It renders the rest of the silver halides inert and they will no longer react with light. At this point you can flip the lights on because you have a permanent photograph or negative, once you wash it off. A fun fact, the silver collected in the film and paper ends up saturating the fixer tray. It is possible to recover the silver from the liquid by chemically treating it and then refining. It doesn't amount to much but it's still pretty cool.

It's usually located on the right-hand side of the board near the top. - CPU power connector (s): These smaller connectors provide additional power to the CPU. Depending on the motherboard, there may be one or two of these connectors. - DIMM slots: These slots are used to install RAM modules on the motherboard. - PCI Express slots: These slots are used to install expansion cards such as graphics cards, sound cards, and network cards. - SATA connectors: These connectors are used to connect storage devices such as hard drives and solid state drives. - USB headers: These connectors are used to attach USB ports to the motherboard. They are often located near the bottom of the board. - Front panel headers: These connectors are used to connect the power button, reset button, and other front panel buttons and indicators to the motherboard. - Fan headers: These connectors supply power to the cooling fans in the system. They are usually located near the CPU socket and the expansion slots.

article: I stepped out, dizzy and dehydrated, shielding my eyes from blinding bright lights. My head was spinning like a carousel as I tried to find a place to sit down and re-arrange my senses. A grim looking chair, with metal cuffs on the arms, and an ungodly looking metal thing jutting out from the top had to suffice. I slumped into it, clutching my head, breathing deeply. I didn't think too much about what the device I sat in was for. I didn't really think about anything at all, to be honest. It took a minute for me to actually start looking around and start to comprehend my surroundings. White, sterile walls, quiet beeps and whirrs, strange devices strewn about the room, Pieces of paper, with frantically scrawled notes strewn about the tiled floor. I was in the centre of a genius's workspace. Removing my hand from my head, I stood up, walking around, trying to find some substantial evidence as to why I was here. Something was missing. I felt that if I saw one little bit of information, one tiny thing, I would figure out what was happening. Or, more importantly, who I was. It was by this point I realised that I was stark naked, and quickly grabbed a towel hanging off a table on the right side of the room to save my embarrassment. After I wrapped the towel around my waist, I paused for thought. ' Why would I be embarrassed? There's no one here.' But, certainly, there was someone here earlier. A cup of coffee, still steaming, sat on the table. A Computer on the opposite side of the room was switched on, prominently displaying a document containing a wall of text. I decided to investigate further. Sitting at the computer, I scrolled through the text, which seemed like a sort of speech that one would present to an audience, and, through the eloquent wordings and descriptions, I figured out two things. One, this room belonged to a scientist. Two, they were on the verge of a breakthrough. This breakthrough in particular interested me, partly due to my curiosity, but mostly due to the way they described it as " The most astonishing breakthrough in scientific history. " Suffice it to say, I wanted to know what was at work in this den of science. Before I walked back to the table, to take a look at some of the documents, I looked back to where I entered the room, and proceeded to kick myself for not looking before. A giant, steel, behemoth of a machine met my eyes. Two pods, each with a door, were connected to a huge box of blinking buttons and flashing lights. One pod, presumably mine, was already open, with the dark, chrome interior being fully illuminated. The other pod was still closed. After taking my good look at the machine, I turned to the table, picking up a note with copious amounts of equations, underlinings and encircled passages scattered across the page. Not one thing pointed to what the ' breakthrough'might be. Page after page, only numbers and calculations met my eyes. I was on the verge of giving up, until I noticed a whiteboard next to the computer. Two big words made everything very clear. " Cloning Experiments. " And there it was. There was the answer I was looking for. I, or should I say, they, had managed to clone themselves, and I was the result. Scientific breakthrough indeed! I looked back at the great machine. The second pod was still closed. Jogging towards it, I smiled, gripping the handle, and pulling open the door, readying myself to greet whomever was inside. Dead, empty sockets. Grey, peeling skin. Thin, loose hair. I was dead. I'd failed miserably.

article: Not only do different age groups need different amounts of sleep, but sleep needs are also individual. Just like any other characteristics you are born with, the amount of sleep you need to function best may be different for you than for someone who is of the same age and gender. While you may be at your absolute best sleeping seven hours a night, someone else may clearly need nine hours to have a happy, productive life. In fact, a 2005 study confirmed the fact that sleep needs vary across populations, and the study calls for further research to identify traits within genes that may provide a "map" to explain how sleep needs differ among individuals. Another reason there is "no magic number" for your sleep results from two different factors that researchers are learning about: a person's basal sleep need - the amount of sleep our bodies need on a regular basis for optimal performance - and sleep debt , the accumulated sleep that is lost to poor sleep habits, sickness, awakenings due to environmental factors or other causes. Two studies suggest that healthy adults have a basal sleep need of seven to eight hours every night, but where things get complicated is the interaction between the basal need and sleep debt. For instance, you might meet your basal sleep need on any single night or a few nights in a row, but still have an unresolved sleep debt that may make you feel more sleepy and less alert at times, particularly in conjunction with circadian dips , those times in the 24-hour cycle when we are biologically programmed to be more sleepy and less alert, such as overnight hours and mid-afternoon. Halfway to work the rain began to slow, degenerating into a mist. Off toward Jersey I heard thunder rumbling and grinned. Jersey is where bad weather belongs. They're made for each other. I always saw her around here. A girl with light grey hair, her eyes a shade lighter. It never struck me to talk to her. She was a goddess, I was a mortal. A little overweight, scruffy beard covering a budding under-chin, glasses. My prime days physically speaking were almost a decade ago as a running back on my high school football team. Adulthood hit me hard. Stress, man. College, debt, hunting for a job, retiring nightly to an empty apartment (or bringing some short-term girl back from time to time) all took their toll on me. Periodically I'd get depressed by it all, generally within a few days of paying what I could off the top of my student loans. Today, though, as I approached the park, I wanted to see her again. In the least sexual sense and in the most sexual sense I found her form pleasing to the eye. She was beautiful, but something told me that I would love her for more than that..... if I could ever open my mouth and say something. I began to lose hope when at last she rounded the corner and walked toward me. Her cell phone was rooted to her ear, hidden beneath those grey locks, curled at the ends today. She wore a long raincoat over black jeans and a white shirt. As always, my heart fluttered at the sight of her but my brain stalled out. I just glanced up at her, and back down before she saw me looking. We crossed paths at the entrance to an alley. Fortunately I'd looked away, like a damn coward, because I saw the car backing down the alley and reached for her to move her aside- the phone was distracting her, and I didn't think the driver could see us because his brake lights were still dim. My hand brushed her raincoat and immediately my eyes whited out. Still, my momentum carried us backward and the car passed us by (I assume) without any harm. By then, my eyes adjusted. Something happened. I looked at the girl, who was blinking and looking around wide-eyed like I was. The world had changed! Black had become something else, and the shades of grey everywhere had turned into other colors, I guessed, but to describe them would be impossible. The world was bright! Our eyes met, hers the same color as the sky above us. There were no words, not at first. It struck me then what had happened. Years ago my parents had told me about this, and I'm sure every parent had said something to the same effect: "Once you find the right girl, she'll bring color to your world." article: As a young man, I had foolishly believed that love could conquer all. Yes, such a feminine idea, but I was gay. I guess that shouldn't matter much, but it does play to this tune. When I was about twenty-seven, I met a man several years older than me. He was everything I wasn't: charming, soft-spoken, funny, attractive. It was no wonder that I fell for him as hard as I did. But it came as a shock to everyone, myself included, when he rejected me only twice before coming to my side one night, asking why I had stopped asking for his company. After several months, we had become inseparable. Two years later, we had handfasted. When gay marriage became legal two more years after that, we married. When he moved into my house, however, everything seemed to change. And it wasn't for the best. He became colder than ever, and was rarely home. When he was, he was either angry, or preoccupied most of the time. We rarely dined together, or shared a bed, or even spoke any more. I could not fathom why things had gone so sour so fast. So, I began to snoop. One day, finally, I found a book in a secret compartment in his writing desk. What I read, I couldn't believe. My lover, my husband, was trying to start a war between anthromorphs, vampires and djinn. I couldn't believe it. My husband had gone insane. And from the dates in the journal, it had been a long, slow progress. I was kicking myself for not seeing the signs sooner, for not seeing that the man I loved was in desperate need of help. I wanted to confront him, albeit gently, with my new knowledge, but I thought it would be safer if I followed him to one of his "meetings" to get video and audio evidence of whatever delusions he was suffering from. I could not believe my eyes when I saw the tall, dark figure approach him from the woods, only his eyes showing in the moonlight. Glowing a soft amber, his eyes seemed to see everything and nothing, all at once, without moving. He raised his head and sniffed, and looked right at me. The last thing I remember before this pain came over me are leering red eyes looming over me, closer and closer, and two small pricks against my jugular.

article: This is where a survey course of art history comes in handy. It's very interesting to watch art move from decorative and idealized to representational and almost photo-realistic. Were humans incapable of understanding depth back then? Didn't have the tools to create it? People understood things like depth and mathematics - you don't get the Pyramids of Giza, Stonehenge, and the Acropolis without an understanding of the world around you. But people today don't seem to realize that there is a lot of mental process that goes on between viewing the three dimensional world and re-creating it on a two dimensional surface. These people were working from scratch with nothing before them to build off of. It's like the difference between a child who draws a picture of a house like [this] (URL0) and Andrew Wyeth's [Christina's World] (URL1) The child sees the world in glorious 3D every day of her life, but when asked to represent it two-dimensionally, she draws a box and triangle and doesn't make the sky come all the way to the ground. These are things that needed to be learned over a long period of time. I'd like to write a whole lot more on the subject, but something that is sort of analogous to the developing language of art is the language of film, although much sped up. I've been watching a series on netflix called The Story of Film: An Odyssey. It's amazing to watch movies go from basically a recorded stage play to something like "Citizen Kane" (I'm only about half way through the series).','The simple answer is that the more people and cultures we meet and experience the more we grow as artists. It's impossible to create something out of thin air unless there is some small inspiration from something else. It's like asking why bands in the 1950's didn't create music that is popular today - art evolves with the times and technology. One final thought - most famous artists now dedicate their lives to creating art. Society weeds out who is good and bad and only the good artists are "known" even though we all doodle now and then. Are we seeing art from primitive artists or from the general population? If someone found my notebook in 1,000 years would they think all our art is terrible because they are basing it on the drawings of me, a non-artist?', "The painters that created those beautifully detailed paintings didn't just sit down at a blank canvas and paint it. They used techniques that helped them, which were developed by people in the past and shared. For example, ways of sketching out the scene to help get the perspective right. Some painters even used tools such as light boxes, mirrors, etc. In short, there's room for innovation and invention in painting, and so there are things that more recent painters had access to that ancient painters did not.

article: We prepared for every eventuality. We walled the entire town with an impenetrable barrier only broken by a sturdy gate, manned 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Weapons stations were positioned every thirty feet, and every citizen carried at least one gun and one knife at all times. Food and water, blankets, generators, ammunition, medicines, barrels of gasoline, all were stored in secure underground bunkers. In fact, the only structures above-ground were watch-stations and training yards. All the rest was meticulously managed plots of land, already producing enough food to sustain the entire town, and rows upon rows of solar panels. A fully functioning sewage system was installed.Living quarters were located in a network of bunkers and corridors underground, fitted with air vents, air filters, and automatic locks timed to match our strict schedules. We drilled daily, and every person, child or adult, was rigorously trained and expected to adhere to the structure that the town ran by. Curfews were enforced. We were safe, completely sealed off from the outside world, save for a carefully monitored communications system, updating us regularly on the efforts of epidemiologists all over the world. We all took shifts in there, flagging the WHO's alerts of possible outbreaks of disease. We knew we were mocked, but we knew that in the end, we would be the ones with the last laugh. For all our preparation, though, it still took us by surprise. And I, I am the only survivor. This is my story. I shouldn't have survived, really. It was only chance that I was kept awake by nightmares, unable to find peace. I tossed in my ship-shape quarters long after the rest of the rest of the'town' was asleep. I could hear soft breathing from my neighbors; doors were impractical down here; we found what privacy we could behind curtains. Afraid of further nightmares, I slipped from my bunk, taking caution not to disturb the two others on the bunks below me. Company would distract me from the terrors in my subconscious, I remember thinking. So I padded through the corridors, my bare feet whispering on the grating beneath, to seek human comfort in the Communications shack. I punched my number into the code-box beside the only door in the entirety of the living quarters. The door opened with a hiss, and the rhythm of sleepful breath was replaced with the sound of gentle static and hushed conversation. The door closed quietly behind me. I was greeted with a nod by the man and woman on duty, but otherwise they paid me little heed. It was not uncommon for sleepless occupants to drift to the communications room at the darkest hours of the night. I regarded the screen idly. Nothing stirred, as usual. It was comforting to watch, assurance that we were safe. The woman broke me from my distraction. "You mind holding fort for us for a few minutes? We're going to make ourselves fresh coffees. Can bring you one too, if you like." I waved my hand in acknowledgement. She and the man exited the room, leaving me to keep an eye one the faintly flickering display. The time in the corner read 3:08. I must confess, I dozed a bit. The next time I looked, it was 4:21. I was alone. Even in the containment of the Communications room I could hear muffled noises from outside. The next shift should have been here twenty minutes ago. Could it be that I had missed the start of the zombie apocalypse? The rest of the town must have been industriously following procedure outside while I, alone and unnoticed, kipped in the safety of the locked room. Furious at myself, I snatched a gun from a rack on the wall, and, feeling ridiculous in my slightly-too-small pajamas, disengaged the lock to join the fray out-side. The muffled noises crescendoed into a thunder of sound. Gunfire deafened my left ear. This threw me, completely. I had expected orders shouted and people to be running to their stations. But not gunfire. Gun use was restricted to above-ground. In the confines of the bunker, the gunshots, so many as to be indistinguishable from each other, roared. I saw blood, heard screams; not the screams of adrenaline-pumped squadron leaders, but the unmistakable screams of dying men. I saw raging, relentless bodies thrown together, biting, clawing, scratching, tearing. The grid was sticky with blood, the air thick with the churning stench of bodily fluids, rent flesh, and sweat. I tore myself from my stupor, leaping back into the Communications room. The sudden silence was oppressive. My heart could not be tamed, nor my breathing stilled. My fingers, usually steady on the trigger, would not cease trembling. This shouldn't have happened. The apocalypse was supposed to happen outside, among the foolish skeptics that laughed at our preparations, not inside the fortress that was our town. My training told me to overcome my shock, to muster my courage, and to stand alongside my dying friends and send bullet after bullet into dead flesh. My limbs disobeyed. They scrabbled at the grating on the floor, and when it came up I threw myself into the space it offered. Had I followed my training, I would have died heroically and horrendously. I would have been shredded by cruel, mindless beings once my family. Instead I dragged myself down miles of pipe, sobbing the whole way, unable to erase bloody images from my retinas. When at last I crawled into clean moonlight I could only lie on the ground and stare back at the mighty walls of our town, our fortress. No my town. My fortress. Their tomb.

Now, when your blood rushes past the arterioles (very small blood vessels; since they are small, they are very numerous, and the volume:surface area ratio is very small, which makes it much more efficient), that CO2 is switched with the O2. Why? O2 has a much higher concentration near your lungs than it does at your muscles; the molecules want to reach an equilibrium. When there's much more O2 in one side, they actively want to get to another side. I'm sure you've learned of stuff like osmosis and diffusion. This is just osmosisdiffusion through the membranes of the blood vessels. Now, the O2 rich blood will go to your muscular arterioles. There, where there is much more CO2, the O2 will be switched. Now, your muscles have O2 to use, which will be turned to CO2 through cellular respiration (IE, how we turn sugar into energy). However, the blood will now have less O2 and more CO2, and we are brought back to the beginning.,The only "nutrient" that a healthy red blood cell carries to the peripheral cells is oxygen. Basically, it carries oxygen around in a big container inside of it called hemoglobin. When the RBC reaches the capillaries, which are the blood vessels with the smallest diameter, the container opens up and the oxygen diffuses out of the RBC and into the surrounding blood. Then it diffuses into the cells in that immediate vicinity. The way this happens, and the reason that it happens are a bit complex for an ELI5 post but essentially, there are many different conditions that alter how loosely or tightly closed the hemoglobin "container" is. article: I want to make clear that I'm not talking about whether Bitcoin will become a (or the) global currency, nor am I talking about its merits as a speculative investment. I am imagining a world where a sizeable fraction of the world's transactions (let's say 40) are made in Bitcoin, and Bitcoin is used as a reserve currency by at least some governments, etc. Basically, it becomes as universally accepted as USD, Euro or RMB. I think that this would be a disastrous economic trap for the world to fall into because of deflation and the Tobin Effect. Bitcoin prices are rising at the moment because people like it or they want to use it as a speculative investment, but this effect will level off with fewer new buyers if Bitcoin becomes a stable, global currency. This is not what I am concerned about. Since the supply of new Bitcoin is designed to drop off asymptotically according to a pre-set algorithm, the rate of creation of new Bitcoin will rapidly drop below the rate of real growth of the world economy. At this point given that PVMY] , there are a few possibilities: 1- velocity of money could increase steadily at a pace which will make up for the difference between real growth and growth in money supply. While there are many factors which can cause velocity to increase or decrease, I know of no way that a long-term, stable, predictable increase in velocity year after year can be created. 2- The world will go into zero-growth mode. GWP flattens out, we simply stop growing our productive capacities as a species. 3- Bitcoin goes into long term deflation at a rate approaching real GWP growth about 4 per annum for the last decade] .) I think that 3 is by far the most likely, and I think we have very good reason to believe it would be a disaster. First, I think that once this deflation begins in earnest, most people are going to convert their savings from inflationary currencies to Bitcoin - why not hold your money in the currency that appreciates? As nice as it is to have your money become more valuable year after year, it would destroy a huge swathe of useful investment opportunities. Imagine you wanted to loan some money to your friend. Deflation is 4, but you think that 4 is too high a rate to charge a friend, so you agree on 2. How will this work? You give your friend the money, and she pays you back later... with less money. You have paid her for not letting you access your own money. This might already be true when lending below interest rate, but think about what this does to a global market when nominal interest rates will routinely drop below zero. You will keep finding situations where parties with money to invest and parties with profitable investments seeking capital will be unable to come to the same sorts of mutually beneficial deals they would be able to make with an inflationary currency. This effectively will wipe out the viability of even the safest investments if the rate of return is less than the rate of deflation. The higher yield investments will not be spared this drying up of liquidity either - high return can only be maintained by high risk, and the average investor is going to be much more wary of investing in a long shot for higher returns if the effort-free, risk-free default of hoarding cash has such a high return. Basically, this is like the difference between investing in capital and investing in land - investing in capital actually brings new productive capacities into being, buying land merely reshuffles the ownership of a fixed resource and pumps up prices. I think that the net result of all this will be a higher rate of aggregate savings, but without the nice by-product of having lots of nice new productive capital making us richer and keeping up aggregate demand, as happens with an inflationary currency. It would also be extremely difficult to undo this transition if we switched to Bitcoin - any individual or group (presuming they didn't have some massive market power to affect others' incentives) which switched back to inflationary currency would only impoverish themselves for no greater benefit if everyone else stuck with Bitcoin. TL;DR - I think the deflationary nature of Bitcoin would impede useful investments and drive the world back to the high-tech equivalent of stuffing their money under the mattress.

article: So, here's the idea with the fifth amendment. It isn't meant to protect the person invoking it, but to protect everyone else. Everybody deserves a right to their own, fair trial. In that trial, they get to gather witnesses, evidence, sit for examination, etc. The fifth amendment protects you while you are testifying at someone else's trial. So let's say that someone is accused of murder, and that they have an alibi, but that that alibi is that they were buying drugs at the time across town. You want to be able to call the drug dealer in to corroborate that alibi. Without the fifth amendment that dealer is never going to agree to testify, and a man will go to jail for a crime he didn't commit. Now that drug dealer can come out and say where and when he met with you and corroborate your alibi, but if asked'Are you a drug dealer' he can plead the fifth amendment - whether or not he sells drugs isn't the topic of this trial and shouldn't be discussed here.,Unless your lawyer has specifically advised you to say something, you should always plead the fifth. You know that whole "anything you say can and will be used against you in a court of law" thing? It's not a joke. Literally anything you say can be twisted and used against you or someone you know. And if you actually are guilty, it keeps you from incriminating yourself accidentally.', "Always. You never say anything unless your lawyer tells you to. Same with talking to cops. Don't do it, they are trying to trick you and they will lie to you.," "In any case where you aren't sure how your words might be used against you. There's a limit between pleading the fifth and being an asshole; but in general, an innocent person is best of cooperating with police WITHOUT giving the police anything they don't have a reason to get. For example, if a policeman pulls you over for speeding, you want to cooperate with him, but don't ever mention how fast you were going, whether or not you were looking at your speedometer, etc. Likewise, he can't search you car unless he has a reason, but if he's asking about something innocuous, get it out and show him. (Note: I am not a lawyer: do not take this as legal advice)

And just forget prom, or anything along those lines. Girls treated me with the same ignorance as the guys. I once heard someone say the opposite of love isn't hate; it's indifference. Sounds legit to me. So I decided I would do something to make them notice me. I've got the gun tucked away in my school bag. Between a science textbook and my lunch.
