I can't exactly ask anyone. Maybe, if I change my mind at the last minute and decide not to take my own life, there'll be support groups I can join. I've decided that the best time to do this is during the afternoon assembly, when all the students gather in the auditorium to hear announcements and whatever. Most bang for my buck that way. But it does mean I need to keep the gun concealed until then. This amuses me more, like I have a special secret. I spend my lunch in the library. The lady who works there, Donna, has never been outright mean to me, but I think she thinks I'm weird. I'm pretty sure she isn't allowed to actually say anything though. So this is where I always eat lunch. No one to judge me here. It's getting closer to the end of the school year, which means exams are coming up, so there's more people here studying than normal. There's Jack in the corner. I'm not really convinced he knows how to read, but his beautiful girlfriend, Jenny, is sitting with him. I guess she's reading to him. At another desk, there's Anna, shy and quiet with huge glasses. She reminds me of an owl. I didn't think she'd ever need to study. Must be about 18 people in here today. About 15 more than normal. I scan them all, and again I'm amused. They don't know what's coming. What would they do if they did know? I stand up to get ready to go to my next class. Just one more to go before the deed. At exactly the same time, I see Adrian Denny stand up from his desk. Another loner, Adrian does more to separate himself than anyone I know. He's gone for a bit of a goth look, and he's the only kid I know in our school with a tattoo. We lock eyes for a moment. He starts to slowly reach into his bag, and it's like everything is in slow motion. Somehow, I know what's coming. I see a glint of metal as he pulls his hand out, and I yell ' GET DOWN!!' Some are quicker to react than others. Anna quickly dives under a desk, and I see Jack trying to pull Jenny behind the librarian's desk. She isn't fast enough, and the first shot rings out, making its way right into Jenny's perfectly tanned leg. The screams start then, and I can see there's a divide between people who are trying to exit the library, and those just trying to hide. The people trying to get away get the next tirade of bullets. Becky and Mason go down straight away, their wails adding to the cacophony. Alex gets grazed by a bullet, but carries on, getting out of the room and sounding the alarm in the hallways. ' DENNY'S GOT A GUN!' More screams. Everything still seems to be in slow motion for me. Adrian's gone after one of the students, almost chasing him around the racks of books. I know what to do in that moment. I grab a chair, and wait for him. I'm at the edge of a set of shelves, and I can hear him rasping as he chases Tom. Tom skids around the corner, and I give him a nod, and hit Adrian with the chair, with all of my strength. I watch him drop to the floor, holding his nose, which is now streaming with blood. While he's busy with that, I get my gun from my bag. I see Anna looking on, her face a mask of horror, and I sit atop Adrian's chest and pin down his arms. ' It was supposed to be me,'I say. I put the gun to his head, and pull the trigger once.

article: It's hard to counter-argue slippery slope criticisms like this, at least rhetorically, because you can hardly ever rule out future events entirely. But I think we can evaluate what's really at issue here: whether the benefits of a funeral-protest ban outweigh the likely negatives of such a ban. And the way to evaluate that is to look at similar restrictions that already exist, and to compare their legal underpinning as well as their practical efficacy. There are many sweeping restrictions on free speech in the US. The classic one: You can't yell fire in a crowded theater. That's been true since 1919, per the Shenck Supreme Court case which determined that you can't make malicious utterances that immanently risk public physical harm, as would a panic-fueled stampede. It's also illegal to physically threaten a person, to intimidate witnesses, to incite a riot. Certain kinds of abusive speech are considered "fighting words" and are not protected by the 1st Amendment. A Jehovah's Witness called a cop a fascist and a racketeer in a public area after being arrested. The Supreme Court ultimately upheld that arrest. I think saying "Your son was a fag and is in hell" is at least as insulting as calling someone a fascist. It's illegal to campaign within 500 feet of a voting facility, to lie certain officials like FBI, to defame or to libel a part. There's probably lots of other speech restrictions I'm missing here. It seems restricting funeral picketing within say, 500 feet, is somewhat in line with the precedents I mentioned. One could argue that funeral picketing risks violence, just as inciting a riot does. After all, you have throngs of people in an emotionally charged situation. And I think that, if only in the case of funerals, this emotional state - grief - does warrant special consideration and respect. This is dicey territory, because it could be considered victim-blaming, but I think funeral protestors are complicit in violence. WBC predicts they are going to be attacked; they use language maximized to inflict emotional pain; and then they sue the city after they are attacked if the police fail to protect them. So there is an inherent risk of violence that even the "victims" acknowledge and predict. Is this not inciting harm? My second, probably weaker argument for a funeral-protest-500-feet ban would be emotional damage incurred by what is essentially harassment. Again, I'm not a lawyer, but if any are here, maybe they can confirm or reject the notion that strident protest at funeral constitutes harassment. There does seem to be tort law criminalizing intentional infliction of emotional distress in limited circumstances. Could a funeral protest ban be misapplied? An attorney could answer this better than me, but it seems to me that a funeral is a funeral, a special and easy-to-define event. If we've banned campaigning within a certain distance of the polls, which represent another special and easy-to-define event (voting), then why can't we do that regarding funerals? It would seem to be in the public interest to ban such protests, for the benefit of both public safety and personal wellbeing. CMV - Would such a ban be deleterious overall? If so, how?

article: Water is not compressible but air is. So, in air, a lot of the energy of a shock wave will be wasted just compressing the air. But, in water, the energy of the shock wave gets directly transferred into your body because none of it was wasted compressing the water. Imagine you were swinging a paddle at someone across the room. If there was just air in between you then the force would dissipate before it made it to your victim. However, if you used that paddle it hit an incompressible object like a long metal rod, the force would be transferred much more efficiently to the other side.', "This has to do with how momentum is transferred in a collision: If you have one steel ball hitting another of the same size, it will transfer all its momentum, and with it all its energy, to the other ball - as in Newton's cradle. But if it hits a much heavier steel ball, it will be deflected, and with it most of its energy. Shock waves behave in a very similar manner: A shock wave in air hitting a human will be reflected almost entirely, whereas a shock wave in water is able to pass right through a human, simply because water is very similar in density and elasticity to tissue.," "Water doesn't compress, so doesn't absorb the energy like air does. The way to think of is like being hit around the head by a sponge, and then bit hit around the head, at the same speed, by a brick. One will do way more damage.

article: This is a different kind of battle, if it does not fit, feel free to delete...... It happens over and over again. The squad lines up to go, our Team Chief gives a thumbs-up, a loud snap, and he is down on the ground. As I struggle to tend to his wounds, I see the light leave his eyes. We are driving to an Iraqi police station to help train some of the new officers. Everyone in the Humvee is happy. We are talking about going home, the Insane Clown Posse, how nice grass is, whatever. We laugh and joke as we hear a loud concussion and sand, rock, and debris obscure the vehicle in front of us. Children pick through mounds of garbage, in bare feet and 120o heat, looking for scraps of unspoiled food. Bodies lay in the ditch, dead for hours, blindfolded and shot executioner style, murdered because they don't support a local tribe leader. A new widower won't stop crying, and her children look off into the distance. They are broken. It is so hot, everything smells like sewage, human excrement puddles in the streets. Garbage lines the roads, with all of this debris, how do we know if there is a bomb or not? We can't stop at every bag... Boom! Smiles. Frowns. Happiness. Devastation. Dead friends talk to me about lives they will never return to. I wake up. Sweat beads on my brow. My heart pounds in my throat. I look at the clock. 2:12 AM. Looks like another night of no sleep. I get out of bed and do a quick check through the house. Wife is sleeping next to me, check. Daughter is in her bed, sleeping. I notice that she isn't quite covered up and is shivering a little. Her stuffed animal, aptly named " Pink Puppy " is just out of her reach. I place the toy under her arm and cover her back up. She shifts a little and is still. I check the locks. The house is secure. A mix of adrenaline and shame floods through my system. It was all supposed to get better after we got back. It is supposed to be safe here, but I can't get these images out of my head. Life is so much easier when you realize that it can end at any time. Living in the moment was easy. Then you get back home and time stretches out before you, as the past pistol whips you in the back of the head. I am so irritable lately, the slightest things set me off. I can't sleep. My wife doesn't want to talk about these thoughts that I need to purge, and I can see small hints of fear in my daughter's eyes when I lose it over something insignificant. I would never hit her, but I am afraid I do more damage with my voice. They would be so much better off without me. That 450k would fix most of their problems. Getting myself out of the picture would certainly help. Work sucks. These civilians have no work ethic, and they are pissed at me for wanting to do things right. You give a lazy dude a little " encouragement " and you are down talking to your supervisor again about " being PC " and " hurting their feelings, " well, his lack of integrity hurts my feelings. I walk back into our room, and reach under the bed. I grab the gun safe and take it out with me to the living room. I quickly punch in the code that opens the box, and pull out my 9mm. Even in the darkness, light reflects off of the firearm's surface. One well-placed shot, and all of this ends. I don't want my family to find me though. When I have nights like this, I sometimes go for a drive. This time though, I won't be coming back. I go back for one last look at my daughter. God, I love her. I hope that she will be ok. Her dog is missing, probably rolled under her blanket; I hope he watches over her. I close her bedroom door and leave. When we were dating, my wife and I would go hang out at a local 24hr supermarket after hours. The lots were always full of cars at all hours. I could simply park there, pull the trigger, and no one would notice. On the drive there, I pass under a viaduct, and swerve the car over to the other side, avoiding an explosion that never comes. Had another car been coming in the other direction, it could have been bad for them. I start noticing every little piece of trash on the empty roads and scrutinize all of it. My senses are hiked up to 1000, for realty no reason, and I can't shut it down. After what feels like an age has passed, I pull into the lot. I pull the pistol out from the small of my back, and look at it. I hear a bark. I look down into my passenger seat, and Pink Puppy is sitting there. Its head is cocked to the side, as if inquiring about what I am doing here, in this lot, at 3am. I set the pistol down on the center console, and the stuffed dog's tail begins to wag. Soon, his whole backside is wagging and he leaps into my lap. He buries his head into my shoulder and lets out a low whine, as if trying to give me a hug. I break down. It is as if a dam has opened, and tears flow down my face as cooped up memories begin to flee my brain. I pul this small, pink-spotted toy into a hug of my own and give over to emotion for the first time in what feels like an eternity. I set Pink Puppy in the passenger seat, and begin to tell him stories of my experiences. He seems to be listening intently. There is the occasional cock of the head, gleam of a button eye, or thump of a tail as I discuss my hopes for the future and fear of the past. I am sure that if anyone walked by and saw me talking to a stuffed dog they would think I was crazy, but, well, I may be. Before long, I look again at the clock, my wife gets up soon for work, and my daughter will need to get ready for preschool. I put the weapon under the driver's seat and place the puppy in my lap. Together, we drive home. On the way, I feel like a new man. I know that I have demons to work out. This isn't a one night and done kind of thing, but we can make it. I try to unlock the front door as quietly as I can and move stealthily into my daughter's room. I look once more at Pink Puppy, smile, and again put him under her arm. She snuggles into him, giving him a big hug. As I walk out I hear her tiny, sleepy voice, " Daddy, when you tucked me in last night, you seemed sad. I asked Pink Puppy to help. " She looks at me, blond hair sticking up in a million directions, blue eyes that pierce my soul, and the sleepy smile of a toddler that makes your heart grow three sizes. I look at her through watery eyes, " Thank you, Kiddo, Pink Puppy helped me to feel a whole lot better. " She smiles again, " I knew he would, I love you Daddy. " and before I can say it back, she drifts back to sleep. I go into the bedroom, lay down next to my wife. I close my eyes and sleep.

article: "I'm sorry, who is this again?" The series of texts I received from the unfamiliar number read like a weird, condensed sci fi romance novel. Professions of an undying attraction - so powerful as to destroy a stellar empire - don't generally appear out of the woodwork when you're a middle-aged shut-in making their living by writing fake product reviews on the internet. "lol, it's me. Katie. From Craigslist, like..... 3 years ago? Already? Anyway, don't you remember Halloween?" I vaguely remembered being at a bar and waiting for a costume contest to begin. I had gone with a girl I'd just met; in an attempt to calm my nerves I'd been drinking, but I managed to overshoot suave and relaxed and land squarely into "WOO! DRUNK ON HALLOWEEN!" inebriation. I became the grotesque, toothy monster I was dressed as; I hobbled awkwardly around the bar, much to the amusement of the attendees and the obvious disdain of my date. You have to work the crowd if you want to win the contest, but what would SHE know about Halloween..... she didn't even wear a costume. Blasphemy. 45 minutes later I was the proud winner of a 200 bar tab. My date was nowhere to be found. I was dragged from the memory by the notification of another text: "So yeah, sorry you haven't heard from me. As I explained, things have been kind of hectic. I totally didn't mean to bail and would love to pick up where we left off!" I smiled a bit, dedicating to a two-part response: "Yes! I remember you! With the fluid dynamics degree, Subway fondness, and intense exercise routine! I just figured that the combination of my drunken jackassery and contest enthusiasm put you off..." " ..... And in a way I wish it had. You didn't dress up for Halloween - being that caliber of party pooper is a deal-breaker in my book. I appreciate the elaborate story you constructed, but I'm not interested." Over the next few minutes my phone beeped plaintively a few more times, begging me to pay attention. Deciding I'd rather not be distracted from my Boardwalk Expire binge any further I shut the needy device off, slid my takeout food closer upon the coffee table, cracked open a beer, and unpaused the show.

article: I believe that The Culture, from author Iain M. Banks, is the best model for the future development of humanity depicted in Scifi, both technologically and socially. If you don't know what The Culture is, here's a [link] to a few notes on it, by Iain M. Banks. Here is a Wikipedia [link] which also describes some of what The Culture is, and is much easier to skim. Here is a short quote from Wikipedia, to provide a quick summary. "The Culture is a symbiotic society of artificial intelligences (AIs) (Minds and drones), humanoids and other alien species who all share equal status. As mentioned above, all essential work is performed (as far as possible) by non-sentient devices, freeing sentients to do only things that they enjoy (administrative work requiring sentience is undertaken by the AIs using a bare fraction of their mental power, or by people who take on the work out of free choice). As such, the Culture is also a post-scarcity society, where technological advances ensure that no one lacks any material goods or services. As a consequence, the Culture has no need of economic constructs such as money (as is apparent when it deals with civilizations in which money is still important). The Culture rejects all forms of economics based on anything other than voluntary activity. "Money is a sign of poverty" is a common saying in the Culture." Generally, I am comparing this civilization to other imagined civs from other sources, Star Trek comes to mind, though it is possible that there is some other imagined society, grounded in some level of reality, that would be an even better model that I have either not encountered, or has not yet been conceived. Essentially, I believe that Humanity should work to emulate The Culture, where possible. I realize that as of today, a lot of the technological, and subsequently, social constructs can not be created (AI, FTL, advanced genetic engineering, nanoscale engineering or megascale engineering), but as we advance technologically, as a civilization, The Culture is the best model (I am aware of) to measure ourselves against, and work towards emulating. If you have questions on the capabilities of The Culture, just ask, and I'll try to answer them as well. EDIT: So I'm reading a lot of criticisms of the Culture itself, and while many have a limited level of merit, I do not believe anyone had really offered a comprehensive reason why the Culture as a whole is still not the best way to organise a society in a future with greater than human intellect AI. article: Balance is everything. Not just metaphorically. Literally, balance is the key to survival when you live on a see-saw. One wrong move, and everything goes to hell. Let me get you up to speed. You see, I live in the city of Equilibrium, which was originally one of the great wonders of the modern world. It was constructed on colossal platforms high above the ground, out of the reach of any of the roving bandit groups on the plains. It was entirely self-sufficient, so no-one ever had to leave for supplies. It was said that Equilibrium would ride out the War untouched. That was true, until the missiles hit. They came out of nowhere, slamming into the titanic struts that held the platforms aloft. The entire city shook, or so I'm told. I was just a baby then. I don't remember seeing sections of the city fall into the mists below, the cries of their screaming residents abruptly cut off. I didn't hear the thunder of splitting steelcrete, the shattering of glass windows, the explosions of ruptured gas lines. All I know is the aftermath. For one part of the city stayed up. Amidst the death and destruction, a single pillar somehow remained standing, balancing a large fragment of Equilibrium atop it. It was never stable, though. The slightest shifting of weight would mean utter ruin. Worse, we had no way down. See what I meant when I said balance was key? I stood on my side of the Fulcrum, watching as James walked towards me from his side. At my feet, a faded and scuffed line of white paint marked the very centre of balance of the entire city. Weight had to be evenly divided between either side, lest one side overbalanced the whole shebang. That meant anyone crossing over had to wait until someone else was crossing over at the same time, thus keeping the balance. The rule was that you had to cross in this street only, so that we could keep track of when people were crossing over. It wasn't a rule anyone broke, anyway. It was that or death. James stopped in front of me and nodded. With a practiced movement, we both stepped over the line in opposite directions simultaneously. I turned and looked back at him for a moment before moving on down the street. His straight black hair shimmered slightly in the sunlight before he moved into the shadow of a building. I shook my head and kept walking. I had to stop obsessing over him. Granted, there weren't a lot of other candidates for my attention in this city, but surely I could restrain myself over one boy? Equilibrium was not a place for romance. It was all about the balance, so much so that even love was subjected to the cruelty of the law of the lever. Stepping off the main street, I entered Harry's Supplies, run by the much-loved Harry Peterson himself. He was quite fat compared to my skinny frame. We joked that when he needed to cross the Fulcrum, five other people had to be going the other way. 'Well, Kiara,' he boomed as I entered the shop.'Still ogling after James, I see.' I silently cursed the man's ability to seemingly see everything that went on in the street outside his shop. It bordered on omniscience. 'For the hundredth time, I'm not going to get together with him,' I said, taking my coat off and hanging it on the hook beside the door.'You'd have to stick us together to get me to go out with him.' 'I probably have some superglue in the back,' Harry grinned.'I'll put some on your palm and get you to shake hands with him, how's that? I still think you two are made for each other.' I felt my ears burn slightly at his words and turned to adjust a display of fruit in order to hide my face. He was right, as he always was. I had feelings for James, there was no denying it. But I couldn't bring myself to tell him how I felt. What if he turned my advances down? There wasn't enough space on this platform to hide away from him. 'Anyway,' said Harry.'I've got a little something to show you, something I've been working on for a while. Follow me.' He led the way out the back door of the shop and up the stairs to the roof. His building was one of the taller ones remaining in Equilibrium, a red brick construction with a flat roof about ten metres square. Usually, the roof was only used for watching impressive lightning storms or drinking cola on a sunny day. But now it housed something different. 'What is it?' I said, circling the contraption squatting in the centre of the roof. It was mostly constructed from bits of aluminium pipe and scrap metal. It had a large roughly triangular canvas going horizontally across the top. I bent down. There appeared to be a small space within the framework of metal struts that could hold a small person. 'It's something I thought could be used to try and get us off this platform once and for all,' said Harry, patting the machine fondly.'We've been cut off from the world for too long, Kiara. I remember the time before we came to live in Equilibrium, all those years ago. You and the other young'uns here, you've never experienced proper grass beneath your feet, seen the world below the mists. This will help you to do that.' I stared at it.'How?' 'You fly it,' said Harry.'Like a bird. This wing here will keep you from falling too quickly, and you'll just float to the ground. They had things like these before the War, you know. Hang gliders, they called them. Best way to get to the ground with what we've got here.' 'So why haven't you told anyone about this?' I said.'Why keep it a secret?' 'I didn't want to get anyone's hopes up,' he said.'It's not been tested. I've built it as well as I can remember with the materials at hand, but I think the others would object to anyone potentially falling to their death. I can't test it; too heavy. It needs a smaller body.' I frowned.'Me? You want me to fly this thing to the ground?' He nodded.'My plan was to attach a cable to the back and let the glider carry one end to the ground. Then we could build a zipline and get everyone else down as well. What do you think?' I smiled.'If this is what it takes to get us off this platform, I'm in. Are you going to tell the others?' He shook his head.'This has to be our secret. If we take the glider out to the edge tonight, we can have the zipline up and ready before anyone can say it's too dangerous. Let the end justify the means, that's my motto.' I nodded and turned my gaze back to the machine that could potentially save us all. And get me together with James, finally. If he rejected me down there, I would have the whole world to run away to. I was surprised by how light the glider was. I could easily carry it above my head as we sneaked towards the edge of Equilibrium. The moon was a sliver overhead; it was as if it too was conspiring to keep us hidden. Harry carried a huge spool of thick cable under his arm. It looked long enough to get to the ground and back several times. The jagged outline of the edge of the platform was outlined by the silvery light of the moon as we approached. I set the glider down as Harry dropped the spool over a bollard near the edge. As he had shown me at the shop, I undid the straps and hoisted the glider onto my back. It fitted snugly around me, the wings jutting out on either side. I redid the harness' buckles with numb fingers, securely fastening myself to the glider. Harry began to fashion the end of the cable into a loop to fit onto the back of the glider. While he did so, I looked over the edge and shivered. The mists below were like an ever-changing landscape, one I had spent countless hours watching as a child. Now I would finally get to see what was below them. Harry finished his work and crept over to the glider on my back. He was just about to attach the loop when a voice rang out behind us. 'A little late to be flying kites, isn't it?' We turned to see a group of men standing several metres away. They were the unofficial council of Equilibrium, the ones who essentially led us. At the front was Edward Heath, a tall, gaunt man in a worn army overcoat. He had been a major in the War before being trapped here and had taken his position as leader of the council in no time. 'Heath,' said Harry.'You followed us?' 'I was curious as to what that thing is on young Kiara's back,' said Heath, pointing at me with the pistol in his hand.'Don't tell me you're attempting to escape again, Harry?' 'Again?' I repeated.'What do you mean?' 'Harry here has been trying to get off this platform for a different reason than what he might have told you,' said Heath.'You see, Kiara, Harry was a spy for the enemy. He gave them the co-ordinates for the missiles that destroyed this city, but didn't get out in time. So he made himself a valuable member of this community to stop me killing him. But now I have an opportunity.' He smiled.'How tragic, that he fell over the edge drunk on this beautiful night. Goodbye, Peterson.' I cried out as the crack of a dozen pistols echoed in the air and Harry keeled over with a groan. I was about to go over to him when Heath looked at me.'Her too.' I took the only option left to me. I dropped backwards off the edge of the platform, plunging headfirst into the open air below. Several shots rang out as I dropped out of sight and I suddenly felt a searing pain in my right leg. But there was no time for that. The glider's canopy caught the air after a few moments and I gradually began to level off. The mist banks below got closer and closer, until finally I was surrounded by whiteness. Drops of moisture condensed on my forehead, chilling my skin and mixing with the tears streaming from my eyes. Suddenly the mist thinned and cleared. I was below the clouds. I saw something tall whizz past me. A tree? Then another. I suddenly saw something dark rushing up to meet me. It was the ground. I hit hard, flipping the glider over and skidding on my side. Then my head hit something hard, and I blacked out.

article: Because "omg spoilers" is an acquired opinion; and if the story is well told, it's also well told the second time. We tend to look for new unspoiled stories in our movietv consumption nowadays, but throughout a lot of history it was perfectly acceptable to ask for as story to be told even though you already knew it. In fact, classical Greek theater makes a point of having the choir TLDR the story before a play, so people wouldn't be distracted by the story development, and could instead concentrate on the Play and the performances. In the Same way, Kids will be able to ListenWatch a Story multiple times, eagerly anticipating it, because they know what will happen, not in spite of it.','Because their brains are still developing, such that it takes multiple viewings of a movie to become familiar with the whole thing. Each time they view it is building on the already-there awareness of the previous times they've seen it, and they notice things they didn't have "room" to notice before. They are also learning to identify patterns and sequences and cause-and-effect; a movie watched several times, with its repetitions of narrative event, challenges and satisfies their ability to go, "first [this thing] happens, next [that thing] happens, and then [this other thing] happens." Becoming familiar with things is a pleasing and engaging mental activity for them, long past the time when adults who are much better at it are either bored or irritated. Of course, oftentimes adults like repeating things too, especially new things that we've yet to become familiar with, but often we love revisiting a good story. It's just more pronounced with young children, who take longer to piece it all together.','Attention span. Things become boring based on how well you know them. Kids, and even adults, can watch movies multiple times and notice new things every time so it doesn't become boring yet. As your attention span increases, you focus in on more details and complete your "picture" more completely with a single viewing. Some people need months, even years, for their brain to "forget" enough detail of the movie so as to enjoy re-watching it.','I think when you are younger repetition does not make things lose their luster as much. There was a sharp whisper of metal edge against leather as the man drew a meter stick from behind him, sheathed in his belt. The teacher took a few steps back, his words failing him as his lips quivered. The student standing in front looked at the shaking teacher, and he dared to move his eyebrows up in surprise. The teacher didn't hit him this time. The caped man stepped towards the teacher, brandishing his ruler. "You have committed an immeasurable sin." He held the ruler in front of the teacher, whose pants were now wet with his fear. "Get away! I'll call the police!" The teacher moved his hand towards the phone on his desk, but the man continued onwards. "And it has come time for me to rule you and with a quick motion of his sharpened meter stick he slashed downwards, cutting off the hand that the teacher had stretched out, incompetent of teaching!" "I am the White Board Man, and it's time to be taught a lesson." He grinned, his pearly teeth shining in the unnatural luminescence of his costume, and raised his meter stick high. "It looks like someone has to school you in manners, young man!" "No! Please! I learned!" He clutched his bloodied wrist tightly, but it wasn't enough to stop the spurting that now dirtied the floor underneath them. "Please!" The caped man shook his head. "You haven't learned. I'm sorry, but I have to pass judgement. With my meter stick of justice, I declare you..." His stick swung down towards the sobbing teacher, cleaving straight into his neck and passing clear through it. " ..... failed." The teacher's head dropped off his shoulders, flopping onto the floor in the bloody mess. The superhero turned around, sheathing his measurement stick and placing his arms on his hips to survey the students. The desks were put back, except for two students who were pinned to the back wall by their desks. The students did not move, and no other student had helped them. Everything was neatly arranged, and even the student who had been failed was at his desk. One of the students, a little girl with two pig tails and big glasses, raised her hand. The superhero coughed, looking around at the kids, who all stared forwards, arms on the desk in the exact same way. He shifted, expecting a response. After a few brief moments, he pointed towards the girl. "Yes, child? I have saved you all from the tyranny of this teacher, what say you?" "Are you the substitute teacher, sir?" There was a moment's pause. And then he laughed, a hearty laugh that echoed once more through the room. "No! My job here is done, I have ended unfair treatment, and now I must go to right more wrongs in many many more classroms just like this one." The girl nodded, and placed her arms down gently, exactly in the same position as all the other students. The superhero took one last look around the room, smiling, and jumped back into the whiteboard with a whish of his cape. article: Ducked behind the register, I slowly move to my elbows and begin shuffling my body towards the employee restroom. The sweat stings my eyes. As I pass underneath the ventilation, my hair turns cool and I catch my breath. Focusing on my only objective, I desperately inch towards a seemingly weightless door. In my left hand I clutch a silver bracelet with it's pricetag still attached. I carefully set it a foot to my left, against the base of the kiosk. I wipe my hand on my jeans, and situate myself away from the store front. I can still hear the fear in their heavy breathing. Their hands gripping the surface glass shaking the loosened wall case. The foul aroma of urine wafts around the register. Each and every move is carefully planned. My right hand rests gently on the swivel door, and I press against in. It glides in silence, to my relief, and I methodically twist my way in. I let the door shut on my thumb, and slowly drag it into the dark with me. A faint glow from one of the stalls catches in the corner of my eye. When I turn to face the toilets, I see nothing. I hear absolutely nothing. Suddenly, a small weight on my back tugs my flannel shirt. The sensation leaves me when I stand to face the shut, blank door. A small handkerchief sits at my feet. I pick it up and roll it in my fingers. My shaky right hand struggles to remove the phone from my pocket, and I place the fabric over the screen. Upon pressing the top button, the microfiber cloth reads "Dr.Optic." I step my way into an open stall and face my left. A faint voice creaks as I perch my body and feet onto the porcelain. "Was someone shot?" My breathing slowed, and I hear a resounding droplet hit the water beneath me. My phone reveals a red swirl. My right shoe proves wet. "Yea." In a fraction of a moment, the gravity of the past four minutes sets upon me. Another drop touches the side of the bowl and rolls into the pool. My foot sticks as I swivel it along the lid. "Why" I couldn't tell if she asked a question. She could be even more unsettled than me. I monitor the doorway through the stall's gap. No noise. "I don't know." My friends. They'll probably resent me for this. Call me lucky. If they hate me afterwards, then at least there'll be an afterwards. My greasy left palm slides down the ceramic divider causing a terrible squeak. Muffled footsteps grow louder. I take in a shaky breath and hold it as my eyes bulge open. Completely fixed on the door, they immediately water, and a tear rolls across my cheek. The door flies open. "POLICE! Hands on your head! Down to the floor!" I cough out my air and clench my eyelids. My feet come to the floor and I lean out the stall. My hands clasped in prayer atop my head. Mike sobs outside in the vestibule. The now illuminated restroom reveals a young girl crying on the floor opposite. Hands frisk us both across our legs. "Jesus. You kids alright?" Before I can nod, she presses into the policeman's collar and tears pour freely from her eyes and nose. I simply stare into his partner's eyes, unsure of what to say. A radio crackles to life. "Perp one, deceased. Second in custody. Over."

article: The men scrambled around as I drifted in and out of consciousness. Chattering away in urgent unfamiliar tones, they had dragged me from the sea's lapping waves, tentatively tapping my face to check I was still alive. As a journalist, entry to North Korea is forbidden. Try as I might, and with the full weight of two top media agencies, there was no way I would be able pass through its gates by land or air. My editors had given up quickly - after all, it was my idea. I wanted, needed, to bag the story of 2015. How the real people of North Korea live. And if I won a prize in the meantime it wouldn't hurt the CV. A sea gypsy's boat, if you could call it that, had taken me as far as it could, but I was still miles from shore. I underestimated the tide on the approach and ended up trapped in a sandbank. I had no choice but to call for help, blowing my plan to stealthily trek the hundreds of miles to where the atrocities happened. I'd lost my camera. My phone was sitting on the sea bed. My editors had refused me the chance to take leave from work, so I told them I was headed to a writer's retreat. A digital detox. They wouldn't even begin to know where to look. As I contemplated my fate, my mind swamped with memories of survivors' stores. Mothers ripped from their children's arms. Fathers forced to choose which son to murder. Perhaps I would be a bargaining tool. More than likely, I'd be made an example of. I tried to fight against the men, who'd surrounded me and were dragging me viscously to my feet. As a pint-sized woman and as much as I loved a workout, the years of manual labour these farmers were forced to endure had given them unmovable strength. "You," I said, loudly, with as much authority as I could muster in my voice. The men stopped. "You. You want money?" They glanced at each other. "I, me, have money. Lots." I held my hands up, slowly reaching for my waterproof clip-on wallet. I pulled out more money than these people would earn in a decade and threw it over. "Take." I smiled, trying to remain unthreatening. They had power now, but money rules the world. "Dear woman, what are you doing?" I jumped, taken aback at those words. The man, the wizened old farmer, spoke in English. Perfect English. "I'm sorry, I didn't..." "Oh," the other chimed in, a smile greeting his lips as he gathered the money strewn on the floor. "Oh she's AMERICAN. One of those. Makes sense lads." "Let's take her to get freshened up. She'll want to meet the other journos who thought they'd sneak in to'hell' to get their story!" The men laughed playfully, and pity hung over their faces as they saw my hands start to tremble. We walked along a dirt track, my muscles aching from the battle to stay afloat in the brutal sea. I had to know. Needed to know. "You understand English." It wasn't a question. I tried to ensure my voice remained strong, but it wobbled. I coughed and sea water spilled from my mouth searing my throat. The man who'd been first to reveal his English accent spoke again, handing me a freshly pressed handkerchief. "Yes dear. We do. It's taught in all our schools. We learn from a young age how to articulate and enunciate in our mother tongue, as well as an array of other languages. Mandarin, Tagalog, French..." Schools? I stopped walking. "You, you go to school?" "Well, not by your standards, which are on a par with Amazonian tribes I'd say!" The men all laughed. Their scathing tones burned my ears, and a mixture of rage and fear bubbled in me. "Our schools are more like your rich countrymen's offerings. They are private. We go to school, learn languages, maths, the sciences, art... everything and anything you could wish to turn your hand to." The second farmer held my elbow as we carried on walking the path. "You see, he said, gently, "We love our country, and our Dear Leader." "How can you love that man? That murderer! He walks around like a god on earth while his people - you! - starve!" Standing in front of the men, blocking their path, I saw their faces change. Insulting their god-king would be what killed me. "HIM?" The third man spoke, before they all broke out laughing. "Oh isn't it wonderful doing this?" the first farmer said to his friends. "That god-king, as you so incorrectly call him, is our ruse. He's what takes your attention. He's our trickster, and you are our mark." I shook my head. "No," I said. "No. The reports, from your people who escape your camps. You fear him." As we reached the end of the gravel path, the men remained silent. The stones turned to asphalt, and sitting obscured by leafy green trees was a brand new car. Not a cart powered by wood or a collection of ramshackle bikes. A car. Shiny and clean. The men stopped. Two entered the sedan. The first man leaned up against it as he stretched his arms above his head, resting them folded on his chest. "Your nation, all nations of the world. They are dirty." He shuffled on his feet, getting more comfortable. "Imagine your friend and you both have a prized vase each. It had taken centuries to create, and was now yours." I looked at him, as tears graced his eyes. "Your friend. He's not clever. He doesn't appreciate it's value. He let's everyone see it, touch it. His friends don't see the value, so they crack it. Before long the porcelain is stained, the vase is damaged and it can never be what it was. It can be fixed, but the cracks will always be its weakness. That, that is the world and every land in it." I heard the trill of a mobile phone, and one of the men in the car answered, speaking Korean. "So we're all broken?" I asked. "Yes. The wars and violence, your lack of care for the weak and elderly. The orphans abandoned by your state and the widows forced out of homes. You weaken your people from birth, brainwashing them into believing material goods are success." I snorted. "So this is paradise, right?" "The vase. After seeing what your friend did to it, you decide to keeps yours safe. So when the same friends say they want to play with it, you say it's already broken. They will pester you, and laugh at you for being weak. But they will leave it alone. "Our scientists have cured diseases your people know nothing about. Our students learn skills to ensure they are entertained without the need for your internet. Our old and infirm are housed in complexes to rival palaces! "If we told the world we could cure cancer with a simple injection, you would take, and your leaders would destroy it. Because you place value on money. Your tourists would destroy our land, our people would be forced out of their homes for hotels. We place value on our people." I stood there rigidly, not wanting to believe those words. He opened the door to the car and I took a seat. We drove through towns and villages, passing houses as beautiful as Spanish villas and French chateaux. I spoke up. "All we believe. The poverty and oppression..." "We place value on our people. When tourists visit, they are shown what we want them to be shown. We have a fool parade around with your celebrities. We turn our nation's lights off at night to avoid being seen. The escapees volunteer to leave, knowing they will never see their families again. Knowing they will eventually die alone, as so many of your elderly have done." He looked glassy eyed into the distance. "They are the true casualties of this game." We arrived at a camp, nothing like what I had come to imagine I'd find. "Your people will be told you are dead. Your family can only come here if we stage a kidnapping. Have a wander around your new home. Speak to some of your fellow Americans. Turn your lights off at night. And welcome to North Korea."

There may in fact be more of a net benefit for people's spirituality, from education about our reality than by defending their right to stay wrong. Again, my issue is not with the people who hold the outdated views. The reality is that most adult humans reach adulthood already holding strong views, and won't switch away from them in most circumstances. If someone actively chooses to be incorrect in regards to how they see the world, the best thing we can do is try to educate them. The middle ground is ignoring them completely, hope their children use the Internet and seek out knowledge and that they aren't making decisions based on their worldview. The worst case scenario is defending their right to believe whatever they want. Let's take an example: Bob believes that God is real. Rebecca tries to explain to him the history of religion, and how the belief in God came from not understanding nature and humans requiring a catch-all to explain things. She explains that praying feels good because introspection is important, and how although there is no "thing" watching over him, the beauty of life itself is way cooler anyways. Accepting one's place in the cosmos takes too much humility, and instead of working on that, Bob takes the intellectually lazy approach and just stays with good olde God. The next best outcome is not Rebecca defending his right to hold incorrect views about the world. It's Rebecca not saying anything. If someone defends that we're allowed to believe whatever we want all it does is promote intellectual laziness, and potentially encourages actually harmful views to materialize and propagate. article: When you clap, you send out sound waves. When two sound waves meet each other, they'interfere'. Imagine waves on water when you drop a stone into it. Peaks and troughs of the waves can either add up or cancel each other out, depending on their relative positions. Sound wave interference can be constructive or destructive. When two waves are in phase (their peaks and troughs line up), they will enhance each other and create a louder sound. This is called constructive interference. On the other hand, when two waves are out of phase (their peaks and troughs are opposite), they will cancel each other out and create silence. This is called destructive interference. Understanding sound wave interference is important in many fields, including music, acoustics, and telecommunications. It can also be useful in noise reduction and noise cancellation technologies.

article: Yes, exactly like that. A bit longer answer: ohm's law is more intuitive, V IR. In a batteryoutlet, you have a voltage differential that will push electrons through the wire and create a current. Ohm's law helps to explain the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit. Voltage, measured in volts (V), is the electrical potential difference between two points in a circuit. This difference creates a driving force for electrons to flow through the circuit. Current, measured in amperes (A), is the rate at which electric charge flows through a circuit. The current is directly proportional to the voltage and inversely proportional to the resistance. Resistance, measured in ohms , refers to the degree to which a material opposes the flow of electric current. It is an electrical property of a material that determines how much current flows through it for a given voltage. Ohm's law states that the current flowing through a conductor in a circuit is directly proportional to the voltage applied across it and inversely proportional to the resistance of the conductor. Thus, the equation V IR is used to express Ohm's law, where V is the voltage, I is the current, and R is the resistance. In summary, Ohm's law is an important fundamental principle in understanding basic electrical circuits, and it helps to explain the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance. It is a useful tool for designing, analyzing, and troubleshooting electronic circuits.

After watching semi-popular videos on Youtube of North Korea, it's hard to believe that the modern schools, cinemas, restaurants and places of entertainment are all fake, and that people aren't genuinely happy. I think that a lot of information we get is manipulated. A lot of stories have been proven to be fake (Like the "Kim" haircut, or the execution of his uncle by hounds), and I think that all the other ones, like the ones about the work camps and brutal executions are fabricated too. There is simply too much evidence of North Korea being a neutral place to live in, rather than a hell hole. It might be in the interests of the current media for people not to sympathize with our potential enemy. CMV.

article: a lock out is the opposite of a strike, the owners are not letting the employees work until a new contract is negotiated. The contract between players and owners expired this year. Players and owners needed to make a new contract that would establish how they split up the money they earn (ProfitRevenue). Owners don't want to give up more than 47 of the money that the NBA as a whole earns. Players want 50. Players do not want a hard cap on salary, meaning that teams have a set maximum for total salary to all players on the roster. The owners want to reduce the minimum salary. Owners are also complaining about the economic conditions of small-market teams such as (Toronto, The Pacers, The Bucks) versus large market teams (Heat, Boston, Lakers). The major source of contention is splitting the Profit, the latest deal offered by owners was 49 of the money with a hard salary cap. Players did not like this deal and felt that the union, who is negotiating the deal on their behalf, was not doing a good enough job on their behalf, they want to leave the union (de-certify) and go to court for an anti-trust lawsuit. anti-trust being laws that are suppose to prevent monopolies, which the NBA has on professional basketball in the US.,Decertification is kind of sham to make it easier to sue the NBA. When the players join a union, they transfer some of their rights to the union. But since the union is a group, it can only sue for things that damages players as a group. So the union is basically saying "let's pretend we are not a union for a while." During that time, players can sue the NBA as individuals...and a couple hundred lawsuit has really tie up NBA lawyers. Then, after they get some sort of agreement, they form a wink wink nudge nudge "new" union, and act like it never happened.', "Basically the owners are claiming that the NBA doesn't make enough money and that most teams actually lose money. This claim may be true, but it's somewhat dubious as the NBA won't release all their financial data. The Collective Bargaining Agreement or CBA, which is the contract between the players and owners expired, so they need a new one. The owners want to keep a certain percentage of Basketball Related Income, or BRI, which covers everything from tickets to jerseys to the tv deal. They also want a hard salary cap set at a certain number. The players want to keep a higher percentage of BRI and they want a soft cap, which means teams are only allowed to go over a certain salary based on certain exemptions. It's really convoluted and complicated. The players decertifying means they break up their union so they can sue the NBA. It's basically just the process where they end private negotiations and go to the courts because they can't reach a compromise.," "A bit of background information: just like other jobs, playing in professional sports often includes a collective bargaining agreement, or an agreement between the managers and workers setting the rules for hiring people. In basketball, this includes things such as rules of trading players, contracts, how revenue is distributed, maximum and minimum player salaries, the rules for the NBA draft, salary caps for teams, exceptions to the salary cap, and so forth. The NBA's last CBA was signed in June, 2005 and ended June 30th, 2011. Much like normal contractsalary negotiations, they are are centered around what you would naturally assume they would be centered on. The NBA (the commissioner David Stern and the 30 NBA owners) wants less costs, while the player's association wants highersimilar salaries. The NBA wants a hard salary cap (which means that teams are not allowed to go over a certain total that they spend on player salaries) at a lower level (so they spend less money, which means they can make more) while the player's associations wants to keep a soft cap (which means that teams have more exceptions, so players can make more). The focus of the lockout is about the BRI, or basketball related income. This determines the revenue sharing between the league and the players. It's a bit complicated, but they total amount of salaries and benefits given to players through agreed upon contracts can't go over the amount that they agreed to through the CBA revenue sharing agreement. If, for instance, it's set to 50 and the salaries and benefits of the players are worth a total of 51 million while the league makes 100 million, the 1 million for the players that would go over the set 50 would be given back to the league instead (there is a process where they hold a certain amount from paychecks, usually 8-10, and then they check the BRI and payments at the end of the season). As for decertifying, it means that the players no longer accept that the union is their legitimate representative to the owners. The threat of decertifying would mean that in the event of a lockout, players could bring individual or class-actions lawsuits against the league for antitrust violation, that is, the NBA committed unfair business practices to create a monopoly. Just as a side note, but this has been done before in the Big 4 Sports, most recently in March of this year when the NFL player's association briefly decertified allowing Drew Brees, Tom Brady, and Peyton Manning to bring forward a class-action lawsuit (Brady, et al. v. National Football League, et al.). Edit: For those interested, USA Today obtained a copy of the last proposal (WARNING: PDF) put forward by the league. The players rejected it today. article: Crossposted from a comment on rskeptic I've read David Fitzgerald, some of Richard Carrier, and the criticisms of both and it seems to me that there is a lot of vitriol on both sides. The mythicists take umbrage at being dismissed as amateurs and dabblers and vociferously defend their hypotheses, the historicists take umbrage at the strenuous attacks, and it all gets very torrid very quickly, and becomes very difficult to actually analyze the actual strength of the arguments. So, as a skeptic, I'm sufficiently intrigued by the Mythicist arguments to profess agnosticism as to the Historical Jesus, for the following reasons: There are no extrabiblical attestations of any significant event from the life of Jesus. On the contrary, events such as the slaughter of the innocents, the census of all the Empire are clearly fictitious, and multiple miracles, the triumphal entry to Jerusalem, and multiple events surrounding the crucifixion are absent from all historical records when there's a reasonable chance that some account of them would have survived, had they occurred at all. The synoptic problem indicates that we are working from at most one source that even approaches being primary, and even that most likely written much later, anonymously, and as hagiography rather than history. Well into the third century, pagan sources mostly recount the existence of Christians and document the claims of Christians. This is at best hearsay. attempts to reconstruct the "real" historical Jesus are invariably unprovable and contradictory with one anotherthere is no consensus. While the vast bulk of NT scholarship presumes an historical Jesus, the "scholarly consensus" should be given less weight since for centuries, such research has been largely a devotional undertaking. Jesus mythicism is very nearly literally heretical, as well as figuratively. At least sufficiently that it deserves consideration even though a strong consensus exists that contradicts it. So, we accept the historical reality of many persons throughout ancient history based on much less proof than gospels and various other pagan mentions. So maybe there was an itinerant sage named Yeshua who ran around, gathered a minor following, and was executed for sedition. But the problems above mean A) we know nothing about him and B) almost everything written about him is unknowable or outright fictitious. I look at it as the difference between "Abraham Lincoln" and "Abraham Lincoln: Vampire Hunter." Notwithstanding that there is an historical person that was the basis, the hero version is a myth. article: My feet were bare and uncomfortably cold in the mire. I trudged to my corner with my plastic tools and started working. I had only ever existed to dig out this river. I knew nothing but my cell, the worksite and the dreary path that linked them. When I looked in the mirror, I saw a tall man with a shaved head, always wearing the same grey uniform. He had a small scar beneath his left eye, and several barely healed wounds on his abdomen. They called this man Spade - they called me Spade. But I could never dispel the feeling that I had once been called something else. Though they were now callused and covered with cuts, my hands had once been unblemished. I remembered looking down at them one day at the worksite and seeing smooth skin and well-kept nails. My whole body had ached that day. My skin burned and bled. My legs could hardly carry me on the way to my cell. The days became easier and easier. Yet I wondered, if I had only ever dug, my hands would have never looked like that. There were other signs as well. Sometimes when I worked images flashed across my mind, visions of places that looked nothing like my cell or the worksite, visions of people without uniforms or shaved heads. I knew things I could never have learned had I always worked at the river. It was mostly information I did not understand, on topics I did not recognise. The words were foreign to me, yet they lingered in my head with strange persistence. A male lion weighs three hundred to five hundred pounds. Nitroglycerine explodes in response to heat. Rick Dall sells STF armour. I started carving a notch into my cell wall every time I was awoken by the bell. But sometimes we awoke to the sun's light, other times there was still darkness. The passage of time, and the length of our days, was skewed. On the day when I scratched the twenty-fifth line on my wall, someone new was brought to the camp. He was tall, taller than even I was. His hands were chained in front of him and his walk was hindered by the manacles around his ankles. There was a large smile on his face, which grew even wider when his eyes met mine. They were a startling blue, and held the same fire as that first day we met, when we were both boys and he had pulled me from beneath the rubble. They called him Mud. I had once called him something else. Mud's manacles were removed, and he was given equipment and directed to dig not too far from where I was shifting rocks. He worked energetically, and when the bell rang to signal the end of the day's work, he passed by me to return his tools. It was the merest whisper. " Hello again, old friend. I've come to take you away. "

article: I still can't believe it. But here the fuck I am. In a tiny tin bubble being hurled off the face of the Earth. Yeah, I messed up. I could see why they would want to get rid of me. Lock me up. Put me to the chair. But seriously? Fucking hurled from the planet? Who the hell does that? "You excited?" The voice comes from the dweeb sitting across from me. His eyes are opened so wide it looks like his eyeballs are ready to pop from his skull smear all over his stupid glasses. Our heads are locked to our chairs. Out of the eight of us, I get to stare directly at his psycho face for the entire 20-year journey. He sits there, smiling. He's been smiling since he turned himself in. Walked straight into the police office with sleeves painted in his parent's blood. Was all over the news. As soon as I heard about the Fletcher project, I knew he was going to be the first one on the list. Never thought I'd be on the boat with him, though. "You excited?" he asks again. He smiles so wide I can see every last tooth in his skull. I refuse to answer his crazy ass. "I'm super excited," he says, answering himself. Probably something he has to do regularly. "Think about it! The very first Martians!" "Couldn't they have sent us to Australia, like they used to?" This time the voice comes from the man next to me. "We'd be just as likely to be killed by some new species of monster, but at least we'd have the chance to get laid, first." He laughs, but it seems forced. He's nervous. Don't know much about him, actually. Squeezing my head in the straps, I can see what looks to be a scar down his cheek. At least he had the good courtesy to put on cologne before we got strapped in. Everyone else is quiet. Most of them are still drugged up. I was the first into surgery, so my meds already wore off before our shuttle even launched. They put a bunch of metal and circuits inside us before we got tossed in here. Something to deal with the "environmental factors" on Mars. Whatever that is. A voice starts to play somewhere in the cabin. "Please remain calm and seated. We will be administering a sedative shortly to help you sleep more comfortably as we begin the cryogenic process for the upcoming journey. We look forward to seeing and hearing from all of you as soon as you're awake." The vents start to hiss, but I don't feel anything at first. Things just start to get less saturated, and then, gently, the lights begin to dim. All I see before I'm out is the gleam of the dweeb's glasses, and the white of his teeth. I wake up a moment later to another hissing sound, only this time louder. I open my eyes to see stars inside our cabin. I feel weightless, and suddenly I realize what's happening. The entire thing is falling apart, splitting into pieces. I look over and see the dweeb's seat split off first, and begin to float further and further away from the rest of us. He's still smiling at me as I watch him fall down to the red earth underneath, hundreds of meters below. My seat starts spinning, but I'm still strapped helplessly to it. My body is nauseous, and my throat is so dry I can't scream. The stars spin so fast they look like streaks of white chalk against a blackboard. Suddenly, there's a huge tug, as if a giant just grabbed me mid-flight. My seat stops spinning and jerks upwards, and then the descent begins to slow. I feel it falling, gently swaying towards Mars. The seat straps release from my head, and I'm so relieved I lean forwards. I almost fall out of my seat before I realize I literally have no more safety harness to this craft. It begins to descend further and further, until the redness that was beneath me turns into a horizon. The sky turns less and less dark, begins to saturate and turn orange. Feels like it's being consumed by rust. I lean back into the seat, sickened from the motion, and rest my eyes. How am I still so tired after so many years of sleep? I hear an engine fire up and the seat starts to sway in one direction, a crisp, clear motion. It floats down into the dirt and finally, stops moving as it touches the ground. I open my eyes and look around. I'm in a trench. The walls around me are at least 40 meters high. They look like they're made of loose, packed sand. With how sick I feel, I don't even think twice about the reality of trying to climb it. I get out of my seat. I fall out of my seat, really. The dirt smells of rust, as well. I can't really understand how I'm breathing, or what's going on, but I figure there's no point in trying to. They didn't send me out here for a vacation, they sent me out here to die. Might as well last as long as I can. The path is blocked behind me, so I move forward. There's no way to see what's ahead of me. The walls are so tall, and the path so long that I can't see what's above. I can only move forward. A half-hour later I come to an intersection. I look around me, but every path looks the exact same. I choose to go forward. Might lead me to the rest of the group. Or, at least, it's least likely to lead me back to where I was. This place is a maze made of sad, abandoned red dirt. As I keep heading forward, the pathways start to become more common. The choices are more open. I hear a slight whirring and walk towards it. There's a small rover driving about and I chase it down. It turns on it's treads and looks up at me with a small black ball attached to a crane. A green light fires up inside the ball. The words read: "May I take your order?" "A glass of wine and a steak," I joke. "One moment," the ball responds. "Wait are you serious?" The rover turns on it's heel without answering and drives straight at the wall. The little treads on it start to bend as it approaches, and the damn thing rolls straight up the vertical wall, leaving tread marks on it's path. I sit down and wait for it, and about twenty minutes later a little tray flies down on a parachute. I unbuckle the clips, and inside sits a finger-sized piece of jerky and a little 8-oz thermos. A thin black font on the cap reads "Please do not discard. You only get one." Shit. I open it up and smell it. It smells like ammonia. Double-shit. Should have asked for a Gatorade. Didn't think it was actually going to bring me what I asked for. I look up to where the rover climbed the wall, and I see it sitting there, a smiley face on it's little black ball. The face disappears and new words emerge. "Find me again for your next meal."

article: I often hear people discussing gun control legislation as "common sense," seemingly as a way of getting out of having to actually explain the logic behind them. To me, the most significant manifestation of this issue is the tremendous amount of support for legislation that would disallow anyone diagnosed with a mental illness to own a firearm. At first thought, such a measure seems to make sense. Surely this legislation would make it such that dangerous mentally ill people cannot obtain firearms, making the world a safer place. But consider this. A man returns from active duty and decides that he wants to purchase a pistol to protect himself. The man is experiencing PTSD symptoms, but knows that if he seeks help he will be barred from purchasing a gun, so what does he do? He hides the symptoms he's experiencing and he buys a gun. So then instead of having an armed mentally ill man who is seeking treatment and whose symptoms are being controlled, you have an armed man who needs medication or at the very least professional help. Legislation like this deters people from seeking help for their mental illnesses and puts guns in the hands of more unstable people. To me, that's why this type of legislation makes no sense. article: Incentive is a misleading word. It's just a weight. Let's say it can do action A, or action B 5050. If it picks right, you up the score 5, if wrong, -5. So if an answer should be A, and the AI picks A, it becomes 5545, with a stronger weight towards A being the way to do things. It's not an actual consciousness, so it's not incentivizing like a person. it's just math that reweighs things if it gives the correct output. Here's some previous posts on the topic: URL0,Incentives are basically what the AI wants. It's usually expressed as a number and the AI is just finding ways to maximize (or minimize) that number. Let's say you are making an AI to play Super Mario Brothers. The incentive would be the level count. You can also have several incentives that have different weights. So after maximizing the level count, you might want to maximize the score, or remaining lives, or how far to the right you got on a certain level. Level count is the most important, so moving to the next level might be worth 100 points, and the other things are worth 10 or 20, but that's the idea. One of the complex parts of AI is figuring out how to set these incentives so that the AI does exactly what you want.','You give it a function that produces a value, and you ask it to maximize or minimize that value. Kind of dumb example since it's solvable in other ways, but maybe you're trying to get AI to find you the fastest driving directions between points A and B, with a potential stop off at point C. You give it a way to calculate how long any set of driving choices would take (e.g. a way to plug in: take I-405 south to I90, then east to I-5, then south to US 101, and out of that get "2.5 hours, and then you ask it to minimize that value. That is its "incentive.,'It is kind of like reddit karma, it is all just numbers. If you had an AI trying to learn tic-tac-toe, to pick the first move, you would do the programming equivalent of putting 90 marbles in a bag, 10 each of 9 different colors, corresponding to each starting square. You draw one, make that move, and if you win, you incentivize the AI by adding a marble of that color, and remove one if you lose. The next game, it is a little more likely to make the best move, and eventually all the marbles will correspond to good starting moves.

article: Employees SHOULD describe in as much detail possible what they didn't like about their old job while interviewing for a new one. This question was inspired by a post I recently saw in raskreddit. To begin with, let me state that I'm well aware that the general guideline is that an interviewee should not complain about his or her old job, manager (s) and pay. Don't tell me, "Well, at my job..." Yes, I know there are exceptions, but that is widely regarded as standard by many in the interviewing process. As an interviewee, if I'm leaving my current job it's always certainly because I am dissatisfied with it in some regard. I may want better pay. I may want a position with more responsibility and opportunity. I may see my chances for advancement at my current employer as poor. I may dislike the culture of the company I work for. I may personally dislike my manager and his or her management style. Each of those is profoundly relevant as to whether or not this new hypothetical job for which I'm interviewing may be a better fit for me than my current one. As an interviewer, hearing what people dislike tells you every bit as much about them as what they do. If a candidate says they hate their job because their current boss is a micromanager, and you yourself are an extremely hands-on manager, you may want to consider someone.else. if a candidate complains about "drama" at their current workplace, you can be fairly certain they'll bring a fair amount of it to yours, too. If they say they didn't like the culture at their current place of employment, you can ask them to clarify and assess how it compares to yours. And there are countless others. Therefore, I think interviewees should tell and should be asked what they absolutely loathe about their current place of employment, managers, and so on.

article: I don't believe that puppy mills are morally justifiable. The practices they employ to maximize puppy production degrade living organisms to statistics, and are overall rather inhumane. That being said, what is the role of an individual consumer is this appalling practice? Puppy mills are definitely horrible places for dogs to live. Given that, isn't purchasing a dog from one of these mills saving that animal from the poor conditions in the mill? Therefore, the moral course of action would be to purchase, and save the puppy. In fact, many animal shelters have superior conditions than mills. As an example, I'll use my own dog. Largely because of public opinion and misleading advertising, I chose to get my dog from a shelter. However, while searching for a puppy to adopt, I ran into a distinct problem: there weren't any. Every puppy had been adopted within a few days of its arrival at the shelter I visited. In fact, in order to actually adopt a puppy, I had to stand in line prior to the shelter's opening. Most of them are just curious, maybe even a bit condescending, but I never hesitate to remind them that they are just like everyone else in the world, while I'm the only truly unique human in existence. That pretty well always puts them in their place. Others come because they absolutely want the experience of what it is like to be me. To be the one who is different, whose body and abilities are unique among all of the billions in the world. When I started, I tried to simulate my minimal strength and capabilities by placing them in heavy harnesses, and all manner of homemade contraptions. But I had grossly underestimated the difference between the vast power in a normal human body, and my own limited aptitudes. Gradually I moved away from the physical, and taught myself to guide my client through a meditation process to help them understand my weakness. Lots of them struggle to limit their own natural gifts, but eventually most people can get the hang of it. I answer any questions people have about the limitations of my physical form. We spend a few hours together, and I help them to live those few hours as someone they could never actually be. Just a simple, bare-bones human being. No special ability, just plain. Every one of them is very grateful when they leave, endlessly thanking me for showing them the beauty of such a special life. Of course, they like to show off their ability to fly, or punch through stone, or blast lasers from their eyes. I always used to wish I could do such things, and I spent my childhood in perpetual jealousy of my friends and all of the fun things they could do. article: Rhea packed her suitcase slowly, meticulously. She knew this would be the last time she would be packing it. Ever. The finality of it, now, seemed ironic to her. It included a one-way plane ticket, and a short list of instructions. She started "Space Camp" in one week, in preparation for a launch early next year. The training would go all through Christmas and New Year's. She wouldn't even see her family over the holidays. Rhea tried to comfort herself. There would be many holidays to come; this was just the beginning. She heard a quiet sob from the living room. Rhea felt her stomach churn. She knew this news wouldn't be easy. One can hope for the best but, sometimes, people get overwhelmed. "Rhea?..." The soft voice came from the other room. Rhea dropped her sweater into the suitcase, and stepped into their living room. Lunch was sobbing on the couch, the arm stained with tears. Rhea sat on the lounge chair opposite Lunch, and put on a sad face. It was a few minutes before Lunch had stopped sobbing long enough to get out a few words. " ..... Why?" Rhea's face went from sad to surprised. "What do you mean, why?" Lunch wiped her eyes and sat up. "Why are you leaving?! This isn't what we discussed. We either went together, or stayed together. Not this!" Rhea's brow furrowed. " ..You're right. I felt that way at first too, but neither of us knew that the screening process was going to be that strict. Or that they were only going to accept 1,000 of the applicants. They needed scientists, engineers, and poets. When it came down to it, I think they wanted my mechanical engineering degree, not your Journalism degree. That's all there was too it." Lunch let out another sob. And another. Then she became loud. "That's not good enough! There were plenty of other applicants, other engineers! They don't need you, Rhea! I do need you! Eternity among the stars, or growing old together! But not this! Not this bullshit Rhea!" Rhea felt a tear start to fall down her cheek. "What would you do in my position, Lunch? This is literally a 1 in 6 million chance. A chance to spend eternity traveling the universe, looking for answers to humanities greatest questions. We will outlast humanity, the Earth, the Sun, and the stars! We would be gods! How can I pass this up, Lunch?! Tell me!" Lunch became inconsolable, falling back into the couch and sobbing uncontrollably. Rhea's tears started to fall as well. Rhea walked back into her room, and finished packing her suitcase. She included one picture of her parents, and one of her and Lunch on vacation in New York City last August. Everything had seemed so much easier then. Rhea returned to the living room, coat on, and suitcase in hand. Lunch was motionless. " ..... I'm not going to forget you, Lunch. You'll hear from me at every opportunity. I'll tell you about my life, my hopes, my struggles. I'll tell you I love you. That I miss you. Out of all the people I met here, you were my favorite. The one I wanted to spend the rest of my life with. But..." Her voice trailed off. There was nothing more to be said, that had not already been said. As Rhea walked towards the door, Lunch flew to her feet, her face red and tear soaked. Desperation in her eyes. "Please, Rhea, don't go. Not like this." Rhea opened the door, turned to face her partner and lover, and said, "This is the only way I can go, Rhea." The door shut quietly.

article: That is called bootstrap problem. How can you program something when no software exists that lets you program things. And how can a computer read what to do, if it has no instructions to begin with? One possible solution to the bootstrap problem is to start with a set of very basic instructions written in machine language (the language that computers speak), and use those instructions to build more complex instructions and programs. This process is also known as bootstrapping or self-hosting. For example, a programmer could start with the most basic machine instructions to add, subtract, and compare numbers, and then use those instructions to create more complex operations like conditional statements, loops, and functions. Over time, more complex programs and programming languages can be built upon this foundation. Another solution is to use a pre-existing programming language or tool to create the initial instructions or software needed to bootstrap a new system. This approach is common in the development of operating systems, where code is initially written in a higher-level language like C, and then compiled into machine code that can be run on a computer. Overall, there are several ways to approach the bootstrap problem, and the solution will typically depend on the specific goals and constraints of the project.
