article: The bells of the tower tolls out eight long, baleful notes, matching the rhythm of my heart. I wished for both to stop. Looking down at the man in the casket below me I saw the love of my life, the man who gave me meaning. He was my rock, my soul, my castle and now he was gone, taken from me by a pair of speeding lights on a rainswept road in the night. His dark cheeks were sunken into that sharp jawbone, for even in death he was handsome. Closed eyelids hid those fierce dark eyes that told me: you have meaning. Nothing could stop the tears from running down my face onto the last suit he will ever wear. The bell's final tone rang into silence, accentuating how barren the small chapel was. I had asked my family to come on a whim alone but they have not had anything to do with me after they cursed my name out the house ten years ago. For here I stand, as alone as I was before the day I met Joseph. There is nothing worse than having to go through the things of your loved ones after they die. I couldn't bring myself to do it, not yet. Our bed never felt so empty and cold, every night I cried myself to sleep for without his strong arms to hold me I had no anchor to latch onto and keep myself from drifting away. The writing desk and sheets of paper which he had given me to pursue my dreams left scattered about and crumpled, in my foolishness I had believed that I could be a great writer. Seeing my face in the bathroom mirror I only held contempt for the dull eyes that gazed back at me, the scattered curls, the short brown stubble, every bit as despicable as the last. I don't know what luck came to me on the day we met but I didn't deserve such a kind and caring man in my life. I found his journal on the bedside table. I had joked once about reading it when he wasn't home and instead he left it out all the time, "because I know I can trust you," he said. Now he was gone. Opening it I saw his flowing cursive that put my blocky ten-year-old calligraphy to shame. There was a single line on the first page: ' Time is a river with infinite branches, having no ending or beginning '. He always did have a love for grandiose statements. "I found him. I thought it would be a lot harder really. Like Where's Waldo except on hard mode where he doesn't have his striped red shirt and the picture is an entire town, but there he is. A shadow that no one notices in the corner of the bar, sipping the cheapest beer they offer because I doubt he can afford anything else to drown his sorrows in. I never really took notice of him the first few jumps back in time but I think it's the destiny of all time travelers, dimension divers, whatever you want to call us, to save lives. I know full well it probably won't work, death has a funny way of being irreversible, but feel an endless calling towards the task. If I can just give that man one more day, one more hour, one more second. Then I will be happy. I know in three weeks he will commit suicide. At 11:32 pm, he will jump of the highest building he can get to. I will stop him, I will save him. No matter the cost."

article: Galileo discovered that pendulum no matter how far they are swinging always have the same period (length of time between swings) and for short swings it's determined by only by the length of the pendulum. From there it was trivial to determine the length of a pendulum that would have a period that related usefully to 1 second. With a 1 second pendulum, clock makers built an escape mechanism that allowed the pendulum to control a gear's spin one toothso it advances 1 tooth per second or some similar multiple. (with a weight to provide force to turn the gear when allowed). Once you have a gear that moves 1 tooth per second it's just mechanics to spin clock hands any multiple of that for the necessary hands. Mechanical watches can't use a pendulum, so they use a [balance wheel] (URL0) that uses spring tension and weight to control the rotation time.,While the specifics have changed, the method has not. Basically, we use an oscillation, something that swings back and forth at a known rate, to calculate time. Back in the day, it was a pendulum that swing back and forth in exactly the same period every time. The clock could be "tuned" if it was running fast or slow by changing the weight or length of the pendulum. Each time it swings, it turns a gear, which advances the time by a certain amount. Some careful gearing is all it takes. Big Ben, as an example of a 150 year old clock, uses a pendulum that beats (swings back and forth) every 2 seconds. Even though it weighs 300kg, a single penny has the effect of knocking it about.4 seconds off per day. Precise tuning of this weight can produce very accurate time keeping. It's not hard to realize that 30 swings, 2 seconds each, should move the minute hand one spot and 1800 should move the hour hand one spot-it's just a matter of gearing. Modern watchesclocks use the same idea. The balance wheel acts like the pendulum, spinning back and forth at a constant and known rate (usually, 3 or 5 times per second). By changing how far it can spin, we can also change how long it takes to spin, and adjust the speed until it is accurate. Some careful gearing ensures that the oscillation is turned into relevant time keeping. With a modern mechanical watch, the balance wheel stop being just a fraction of a millimeter out of position means the watch could be quite a few minutes fast or slow. The tuningsetting is just as important as the mechanics.

The squirrel morphs and changes into a tennis ball. Her favorite. Of course. Hey, at least I get to stand still. I throw the ball as far as I can, then collapse on the ground as she gleefully chases it. If the pattern holds, we'll get to go home in about three hours. Then it's belly rub time for about an hour, followed by a hamburger and buttered toast. We have a freezer full of nothing but hamburger, a pantry full of toast. Not bread. Hot, buttered toast. article: Aesthetic image captioning (AIC) refers to the multi-modal task of generating critical textual feedbacks for photographs. While in natural image captioning (NIC), deep models are trained in an end-to-end manner using large curated datasets such as MS-COCO, no such large-scale, clean dataset exists for AIC. Towards this goal, we propose an automatic cleaning strategy to create a benchmarking AIC dataset, by exploiting the images and noisy comments easily available from photography websites. We propose a probabilistic caption-filtering method for cleaning the noisy web-data, and compile a large-scale, clean dataset 'AVA-Captions', ( 230 , 000 images with 5 captions per image). Additionally, by exploiting the latent associations between aesthetic attributes, we propose a strategy for training a convolutional neural network (CNN) based visual feature extractor, typically the first component of an AIC framework. The strategy is weakly supervised and can be effectively used to learn rich aesthetic representations, without requiring expensive ground-truth annotations. We finally showcase a thorough analysis of the proposed contributions using automatic metrics and subjective evaluations.

article: I am strictly a PC gamer. I own an XBox controller for my PC and am very interested in the upcoming Steam controller. But I'm hesitant to make the purchase, as I barely use my XBox controller. I have tried several times to get used to playing with a controller - even reinstalling old games and starting with the controller to familiarize myself - and I always go back to 'mouse and keyboard'. Below are the reasons I think 'mouse and keyboard' is the best way to play PC games (really: any game, but KM is really only an option on the PC). The mouse is infinitely more precise than a controller. I can't even imagine playing FPS games with a controller (mostly, I've been playing 3rd-person action games a la Arkham and Tomb Raider). I know many FPS games use an aim assist system to compensate for the imprecision of a controller. I would rather have a more precise input system than an 'assist' to compensate for the imprecision of my input device. Because we use them all the time, a keyboard is intuitive. Most of us use computer keyboards and mice on a daily basis in our work. Every QWERTY keyboard has the same layout. When a game tells me 'press X', I know exactly where X is. Even people who are very familiar with controller layouts haven't spent nearly as much time with that controller as they have with a keyboard and mouse. Keyboard and mouse work for all games. As I mentioned, I prefer the precision of KM for FPS games. But I'm also a big-time RTS and strategy gamer (Total War are my favorite games) and there's no way I could imagine playing strategy games with a controller. KM works for everything. I even preferred Dark Souls with a KM - a game that many will say is only playable with a controller. I am perfectly comfortable in my computer chair. One of the big advantages I often hear about controllers is the ability to play from the couch. I prefer to be close to my display (I play on a 32in TV and sit about 3 feet back). My keyboard and mouse sit on a laptop desk and my computer chair is very comfortable. I feel more engaged in my games at the distance I sit vs. sitting on the couch. Why I want my view changed: I think the Steam controller looks really cool, but I'm not sure I'd use it. I don't want to make a purchase I won't use. Am I missing out on good experiences that only a controller can offer? I've got a device I barely use. I would like to use it more, if there are games in which using it would give me a better experience. Edit: many good suggestions in this thread so far. I'm going to spend a few minutes playing some of the types of games mentioned (stealth, action, driving, etc.) and see if the controller enhances the experience. Edit 2: Hey everyone. I am going to make it point to use my controller as often as I can going forward, and am still considering a Steam controller purchase. Thanks, everyone, this was exactly the conversation I wanted to have. Please feel free to keep posting, if you have something new to add. I will keep reading, commenting, and awarding deltas. article: We consider the problem of training machine learning models on distributed data in a decentralized way. For finite-sum problems, fast single-machine algorithms for large datasets rely on stochastic updates combined with variance reduction. Yet, existing decentralized stochastic algorithms either do not obtain the full speedup allowed by stochastic updates, or require oracles that are more expensive than regular gradients. In this work, we introduce a Decentralized stochastic algorithm with Variance Reduction called DVR. DVR only requires computing stochastic gradients of the local functions, and is computationally as fast as a standard stochastic variance-reduced algorithms run on a 1 n fraction of the dataset, where n is the number of nodes. To derive DVR, we use Bregman coordinate descent on a well-chosen dual problem, and obtain a dual-free algorithm using a specific Bregman divergence. We give an accelerated version of DVR based on the Catalyst framework, and illustrate its effectiveness with simulations on real data.

article: " Next to the rose bushes. After 8 PM. " The air feels damp as I bury a stale German girl in the rear corner of the garden. From the window of the dressing room in the second floor, I sense the presence of Mrs. Wilson as she stands tall in her evening garment. I stop for a while and stare back at her with a faint smile on my face - it is to acknowledge that I understand the butler's duty; to always be present but invisible, to always know but never expose. Next to the German girl lies an Arab boy, perhaps 15 or 18. It is difficult to tell because he was a meek child with a frail bone structure. Above the Arab boy lies a girl whose life stopped abruptly in her early 20's, and next to her, another girl, and next to that girl, a six-years-old child whose blonde hair and deep-set dimples once earned him the nickname, Little Prince. Upon arrival, the bodies share similar signature wounds; 16 stab wounds to the lower abdomen region and signs of asphyxiation. As I bury the body deep into the grounds, I share a prayer under my breath, " May you rest in peace, my child. May your sins be forgiven. " By next Spring, roses will grow in this spot and hide the secrets that lie within. " Francis, order the cleaners to wipe off the dust on the frames. We don't want to embarrass our guests, do we? " " Of course, Mrs. Wilson. I'll have a word with Jeanne in the morning. " As Mrs. Wilson scurries to her room, I inspect the photos hanging on wooden frames. In one photograph, I see the Arab boy and Mr. Wilson in front of the Ferris wheel. They are smiling like friends - maybe even like father and son - and it is obvious that he didn't see it coming. There's a small framed photo of the little blonde boy and freckled German girl. The girl is holding the boy in her arms at a familiar park, posing to get the photo taken. Her smile is wide and the boy is giggling; his dimples cast a shadow in his tiny chubby cheeks. There are several group photos from different dates. One noticeable photo is set in a room in this house that used to be a nursery. " Few hours pass by and Mr. Wilson returns from his last hunt. The front gate squeaks as he enters with a brown sack in his arms. It is dim inside the house, but I can sense that his suit is damp with the metallic odor of this last kill. I follow Mr. Wilson to the garden. " Take this, Francis. " " Is this the last one, sir? It is a photo of Mr. Wilson and his baby prince - the little boy whose dimples Mr. Wilson once so proudly showed the world - both of them smiling brighter than sunshine. article: I'm by no means fluent in German, but I'll try to explain this the way my German teacher did. German has 4 cases: Nominative, Accusative, Dative, and Genitive. English has 3 cases: Nominative, Objective, and Genitive. Nominative is more or less the same in both languages. It's the subject of a sentence, or whoeverwhatever is doing the verb. In the sentence "I cook a cake," I is the subject because I is who's doing the cooking. Genitive is also the same, and can be summed up as possession. When a noun modifies another noun, that's genitive case. Take the phrase "my dog," my is the genitive form of the noun "me," but in this case is modifying the noun "dog" to tell you that the dog belongs to me. Generally, only adjectives modify nouns. The English Objective case accounts for the last two German Cases. It'll be clearer if I break up Objective into the two kinds of object we have in English: Direct and Indirect. A Direct Object is one that is directly being acted upon. In the sentence "I throw the ball," the ball is what I'm throwing, so it's the direct object. An Indirect Object is one that is not being directly acted upon. In the sentence "I throw the ball to the man," the man is not what I'm throwing, but who I'm throwing to, so he's an indirect object of the verb "throw." A good way to spot an indirect object is to find a preposition (to, from, around, etc) and see what that preposition is modifying, that's usually going to be an indirect object. German took these two grammar constructs and split them into separate cases (English probably did too at one point, but we lost that over time). Accusative is for Direct Objects (my German teacher used the mnemonic "DOA," or "Direct Object: Accusitive, while Dative is for Indirect Objects I OD" or "Indirect Object: Dative.','I'm not fantastic with it, but I'll give it a try. There are cases in some languages that refer to the position or role a word plays in a sentence, and a strong case system can allow more flexibility with word order. In English we have 3 cases Nominative, Accusative and Genitive (or Subjective, Objective and Possessive, for more modern words). In a sentence a noun can be the subject, the object or indicate possession. Think of the sentence "I kicked his football." "I" is the subject of the sentence, so we use the subjective "I," rather than the objective "me" or the possessive "mine." Football is the object, but in English most nouns don't change. "his" indicates possesion (without using the verb "to own, so is in the possessive case. In modern English we got rid of most cases, and the remaining cases are mostly consigned to pronouns (IMe, WeUs,....) but in other languages more are used. The Dative case is the additional one for German (not present in modern English), and indicates the indirect object, the target of the object - "I give an object to him," "I send an object to him." The "him" is in dative (in German), so any rules for dative apply here. In German cases also change the articles before a noun, so a noun in case x will have a corresponding definite (the) and indefinite (a) articles, as well as different forms for preceding adjectives (White, large, etc) and personal pronouns (Ime - you'll be used to that from English) I apologise if anything is incorrect or absent, my knowledge on this is kind of cobbled together. Good luck learning German.

article: We describe a new algorithm for calculating the topological degree deg (f , B , 0) where B R n is a product of closed real intervals and: f B R n is a real-valued continuous function given in the form of arithmetical expressions. The algorithm cleanly separates numerical from combinatorial computation. Based on this, the numerical part provably computes only the information that is strictly necessary for the following combinatorial part, and the combinatorial part may optimize its computation based on the numerical information computed before. We present computational experiments based on an implementation of the algorithm. In contrast to previous work, the algorithm does not assume knowledge of a Lipschitz constant of the function f , and works for arbitrary continuous functions for which some notion of interval arithmetic can be defined.

article: If I go into a store in Chicago, Seattle, and Atlanta to buy a PS4, every price tag will say 400. Every cash register will ring it out for a different price. Each physical store location only has one set of taxes and fees. Taxes tend to be based on the location where the product is being purchased. Practically everyone is paying sales tax when they buy a product at a physical store, so that tax should be included in price tag. It is tedious and unnecessary for consumers to have to calculate taxes on all their items when a retailer has the ability to include these prices without any significant hardships. The retailer is already calculating tax at the register, so it should not be very difficult to calculate tax on the price tags. Now, let's say I want to buy the PS4 from an online store. I can be anywhere when I'm accessing that online storefront. Since taxes depend on the location of the person, the digital store shouldn't be required to list post-tax prices since different people will be paying different prices. If I select my location, the website should show me which taxes I would be paying, but it doesn't know that until I give my location. I got this view after the whole GOG controversy with regional pricing. A digital storefront can offer the same price to any consumer anywhere in the world, but because of regional taxes, some customers will sometimes have to pay more than other customers. This is not the fault of the retailer, so they should be able to show their pre-tax price as their main price.

article: After Disney purchased the rights to the Star Wars universe from George Lucas, they created the Lucasfilm Story Group in order to solidify the canon of the series. In doing so, they decided that the only concrete pillars of Star Wars lore would be the six films and the Clone Wars TV series. They should have simply started over. I know that everyone hears the word "reboot" and vomits in their mouths a bit, but Chris Nolan obviously showed us that reboots can work and can reinvigorate an intellectual property for a new era. Simply put, the remaining pillars of the Star Wars canon are basically a dumpster fire. The prequel movies are, on the whole, terrible, emotionless, nonsensical dreck. I'm currently watching the Clone Wars television series and for the life of me: Darth Sidious' plans to create the empire are fucking convoluted, the basis of the Clone War is mind-bogglingly stupid. George Lucas had no idea about writing interesting political intrigue and in the end we got what we got. I'd also argue that, aside from Empire, the original trilogy is plodding, and butchered by Lucas' continuous edits through the 90'searly 2000's. Putting aside the criticisms of the quality of the separate films, together they make a terrible basis for Star Wars canon anyway: because Lucas basically flew by the seat of his pants in creating the series, there are various issues that make the whole of the canon nonsensical (Obi Wan not recognizing C3P0, the new trilogy turning Han Solo into the equivalent of a climate change denier for not believing in the force, advanced technology like R2's rockets and electricity just up and disappear, midichlorians, etc.). Further, there are decisions that Lucas made (such as the way he handles droid 'personalities' in the series: Seriously, who is going to design a droid army and then give them such inept personalities? All of Lucas' 'comic relief' choices in that universe are cringe-worthy). Obviously, Lucas created some timeless characters and concepts that will always stoke the imaginations of fantasy fans the world over, but the context in which those concepts exist is just a muddy, lifeless quagmire. A Song of Ice and FireGame of Thrones has shown how amazingly interesting political intrigue can be - it's also shown how to handle a array of characters while making them human, interesting, and understandable in their own right. The property also handled the emergence of magic (somewhat like the resurgence of force-weilders in the original trilogy) in a way that is mysterious and entrancing. Applying that level of attention to detail to the Star Wars universe is the true way to improve the property: Not continuing to build on the shaky foundation left by Lucas. TL;DR: Reducing the canon of Star Wars to the filmsClone Wars tv series hasn't increased clarity of the continuity, and in fact has removed the vast majority of actual entertaining media in the canon to about 1.5 films. The rich history and imagination-capturing concepts like light sabers, the Jedi, the Sith, etc. are all begging to be retold in a way free from the shackles of hack-y, schtick-y robots, inane nonsensical plot-points, terrible writing, bad acting and continuity errors. article: It was a calm summer day in the city of Tokyo, and there wasn't a cloud in the sky. People flocked to the pier to enjoy the festive atmosphere brought about by the newly christened "Dino World" theme park, complete with a massive pink plastic T-Rex, waiting to greet all comers as they made their way through the gates. Inside the park, different geological time periods were represented in the form of games and rides. The "Cambrian Log Flume," which plunged you down a massive volcano, and into the waters below, along with the "Quaternary Cruise," which told the story of human history using animatronics, were among the most popular. However, none stood above the "Triassic Turbine," a roller coaster taking thrill-seekers directly through the open mouth of the park's prized Tyrannosaurus, which stood over 150 feet tall, and sent park guests racing down an 86deg incline, reaching speeds of up to 96 mph. A few miles down the coast, chaos had already erupted. Tidal waves smashed against the shore, flooding the streets of the crowded city. A confluence of infrastructure and corpses were carried back into the sea, upon the waters receding. The sun went black, as a shadow was cast over multiple city blocks, and winds began to swirl violently around what appeared to be a building, erected out of the sea, where before there was nothing. Thunder cracked, and lighting struck the form, illuminating the face of a monstrous reptilian beast: Godzilla. His strides spanned 30 meters each, and he quickly made his way into the heart of Tokyo, reducing all things in his path to rubble. A train passed by his side, elevated on tracks which were held up by the surrounding infrastructure. Effortlessly, he separated the train from its tracks, now holding it in his mandible. With a snap of his jaw, Godzilla split the train-car in two. A swarm of helicopters, each armed with two.50 caliber machine guns, blitzed around the monster, attempting to blind it with a keenly placed shot to each of the eyes. article: One of the main problems encountered so far with recurrent neural networks is that they struggle to retain long-time information dependencies in their recurrent connections. Neural Turing Machines (NTMs) attempt to mitigate this issue by providing the neural network with an external portion of memory, in which information can be stored and manipulated later on. The whole mechanism is differentiable end-to-end, allowing the network to learn how to utilise this long-term memory via stochastic gradient descent. This allows NTMs to infer simple algorithms directly from data sequences. Nonetheless, the model can be hard to train due to a large number of parameters and interacting components and little related work is present. In this work we use NTMs to learn and generalise two arithmetical tasks: binary addition and multiplication. These tasks are two fundamental algorithmic examples in computer science, and are a lot more challenging than the previously explored ones, with which we aim to shed some light on the real capabilities on this neural model.

article: Recently, many systems for graph analysis have been developed to address the growing needs of both industry and academia to study complex graphs. Insight into the practical uses of graph analysis will allow future developments of such systems to optimize for real-world usage, instead of targeting single use cases or hypothetical workloads. This insight may be derived from surveys on the applications of graph analysis. However, existing surveys are limited in the variety of application domains, datasets, andor graph analysis techniques they study. In this work we present and apply a systematic method for identifying practical use cases of graph analysis. We identify commonly used graph features and analysis methods and use our findings to construct a taxonomy of graph analysis applications. We conclude that practical use cases of graph analysis cover a diverse set of graph features and analysis methods. Furthermore, most applications combine multiple features and methods. Our findings motivate further development of graph analysis systems to support a broader set of applications and to facilitate the combination of multiple analysis methods in an (interactive) workflow.

article: Modern applications significantly enhance user experience by adapting to each user's individual condition andor preferences. While this adaptation can greatly improve utility or be essential for the application to work (e.g., for ride-sharing applications), the exposure of user data to the application presents a significant privacy threat to the users, even when the traces are anonymized, since the statistical matching of an anonymized trace to prior user behavior can identify a user and their habits. Because of the current and growing algorithmic and computational capabilities of adversaries, provable privacy guarantees as a function of the degree of anonymization and obfuscation of the traces are necessary. Our previous work has established the requirements on anonymization and obfuscation in the case that data traces are independent between users. However, the data traces of different users will be dependent in many applications, and an adversary can potentially exploit such. In this paper, we consider the impact of correlation between user traces on their privacy. First, we demonstrate that the adversary can readily identify the association graph, revealing which user data traces are correlated. Next, we demonstrate that the adversary can use this association graph to break user privacy with significantly shorter traces than in the case when traces are independent between users, and that independent obfuscation of the data traces is often insufficient to remedy such. Finally, we discuss how the users can employ dependency in their obfuscation to improve their privacy.

article: We examine how well people learn when information is noisily relayed from person to person; and we study how communication platforms can improve learning without censoring or fact-checking messages. We analyze learning as a function of social network depth (how many times information is relayed) and breadth (the number of relay chains accessed). Noise builds up as depth increases, so learning requires greater breadth. In the presence of mutations (deliberate or random) and transmission failures of messages, we characterize sharp thresholds for breadths above which receivers learn fully and below which they learn nothing. When there is uncertainty about mutation rates, optimizing learning requires either capping depth, or if that is not possible, limiting breadth by capping the number of people to whom someone can forward a message. Limiting breadth cuts the number of messages received but also decreases the fraction originating further from the receiver, and so can increase the signal to noise ratio. Finally, we extend our model to study learning from message survival: e.g., people are more likely to pass messages with one conclusion than another. We find that as depth grows, all learning comes from either the total number of messages received or from the content of received messages, but the learner does not need to pay attention to both. JEL Classification Codes: D83, D85, L14, O12, Z13 Keywords: Social Learning, Communication, Noise, Mutation, Bias, Fake News, Censorship, Misinformation, Disinformation

article: I'm not a doctor, but the general idea is that stress heightens your fight or flight response, shuttingslowing down a lot of processes to give you more adrenaline and energy. In extreme situations, you get a short burst of extreme power and everything else shuts off. People in extreme situations have felt like time is slowing down, and that they can no longer feel pain for a short period. In high stress situations, animals are more likely to void their bowels. This also applies to less extreme scenarios. For example, this is supposedly the reason why your mouth gets dry when you're nervous, your digestive system is slowing down starting with the mouth. This is fine for short periods of time (and it's definitely necessary if a bear is attacking you or whatever), but if you're stressed for longer periods, that means that lots of processes in your body stay slowed down, like your immune system. There are connections between long-term stress and being shorter because your body can literally stop growing for a while until you deal with stress. Basically, your body has a limited amount of energy resources, and when you're stressed it puts energy toward dealing with the stress rather than other important stuff (like the immune system).,Cortisol is released when you are stressed because of our "fight or flight reaction." While cortisol is beneficial in the short term like if you're punching a bear in the mouth to save your Chihuahua, but if it's long term stress like a crappy job, two kids who hate you and a divorce proceeding, it does a lot of damage to the body. The way it impacts the immune system is by interfering with T-cells, a type of white blood cell. These cells work kind of like the TSA. They scan other cells to see if they are infected, and they help get rid of them or clear them of the infection. Now let's say we start taking away the TSA's metal detectors. Obviously this would be bad as we wouldn't be able to tell who was carrying weapons on their person or not. Cortisol takes away T-cells "infection detectors." article: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) is an emerging paradigm for harnessing the natural dynamics of quantum systems as computational resources that can be used for temporal machine learning (ML) tasks. In the current setup, QRC is difficult to deal with high-dimensional data and has a major drawback of scalability in physical implementations. We propose higher-order QRC, a hybrid quantum-classical framework consisting of multiple but small quantum systems that are mutually communicated via classical connections like linear feedback. By utilizing the advantages of both classical and quantum techniques, our framework enables an efficient implementation to boost the scalability and performance of QRC. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in emulating large-scale nonlinear dynamical systems, including complex spatiotemporal chaos, which outperforms many of the existing ML techniques in certain situations.

article: In computational complexity, a significant amount of useful theory is built on a foundation of widely-believed conjectures about the separation of complexity classes, the most famous of which is P NP. In this work, we examine the consequences of one such conjecture on the combinatorics of 3-manifold diagrams. We use basic tools from quantum computation to give a simple (and unconditional) proof that the Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant of 3-manifolds is P-hard to calculate. We then use this fact to show that, if NP P, then there exist infinitely many 3-manifold diagrams which cannot be made logarithmically "thin" (relative to their overall size) except perhaps by an exponentially large number of local moves. The latter theorem is an analogue of a result of Freedman for the Jones Polynomial.

article: Instrumental intelligibility metrics are commonly used as an alternative to listening tests. This paper evaluates 12 monaural intrusive intelligibility metrics: SII, HEGP, CSII, HASPI, NCM, QSTI, STOI, ESTOI, MIKNN, SIMI, SIIB, and sEPSM corr . In addition, this paper investigates the ability of intelligibility metrics to generalize to new types of distortions and analyzes why the top performing metrics have high performance. The intelligibility data were obtained from 11 listening tests described in the literature. The stimuli included Dutch, Danish, and English speech that was distorted by additive noise, reverberation, competing talkers, pre-processing enhancement, and post-processing enhancement. SIIB and HASPI had the highest performance achieving a correlation with listening test scores on average of 0.92 and 0.89 , respectively. The high performance of SIIB may, in part, be the result of SIIBs developers having access to all the intelligibility data considered in the evaluation. The results show that intelligibility metrics tend to perform poorly on data sets that were not used during their development. By modifying the original implementations of SIIB and STOI, the advantage of reducing statistical dependencies between input features is demonstrated. On the head of the elevator was a phrase engraved onto the metal: "Absence of thought is true beauty." article: This paper deals with two main issues regarding the short polar codes: the potential of FEC-assisted decoding and optimal code concatenation strategies under various design scenarios. Code concatenation and FEC-assisted decoding are presented systematically, assuming a packetized system. It is shown that FEC-assisted decoding can improve frame error rate of successive cancellation decoding arbitrarily, at the expense of some coding rate loss and decoding complexity linearly increasing with the number of codewords in the frame. This is compared with list decoding whose complexity grows linearly with the list size as well as the number of codewords. Thereafter, the frame construction procedure and decoding algorithm are developed in a realistic framework. Taking into consideration the effective throughput of the transmission protocol, the problem of optimal design of concatenated codes is formulated under polar code length, frame length and target frame-success-rate constraints. Simulations are performed assuming both additive white Gaussian noise and Rayleigh fading channels. It is shown that the divide-concatenate strategy for long frames does not lead to any considerable gain. It is also shown that the performance of FEC-assisted decoding of frames is improved as the frame length increases while the conventional successive cancellation decoding undergoes a dramatic performance loss.

article: Understanding images with people often entails understanding their interactions with other objects or people. As such, given a novel image, a vision system ought to infer which other objectspeople play an important role in a given person's activity. However, existing methods are limited to learning action-specific interactions (e.g., how the pose of a tennis player relates to the position of his racquet when serving the ball) for improved recognition, making them unequipped to reason about novel interactions with actions or objects unobserved in the training data. We propose to predict the "interactee" in novel images - that is, to localize the object of a person's action. Given an arbitrary image with a detected person, the goal is to produce a saliency map indicating the most likely positions and scales where that person's interactee would be found. To that end, we explore ways to learn the generic, action-independent connections between (a) representations of a person's pose, gaze, and scene cues and (b) the interactee object's position and scale. We provide results on a newly collected UT Interactee dataset spanning more than 10,000 images from SUN, PASCAL, and COCO. We show that the proposed interaction-informed saliency metric has practical utility for four tasks: contextual object detection, image retargeting, predicting object importance, and data-driven natural language scene description. All four scenarios reveal the value in linking the subject to its object in order to understand the story of an image.

article: Contextual language models (CLMs) have pushed the NLP benchmarks to a new height. It has become a new norm to utilize CLM provided word embeddings in downstream tasks such as text classification. However, unless addressed, CLMs are prone to learn intrinsic gender-bias in the dataset. As a result, predictions of downstream NLP models can vary noticeably by varying gender words, such as replacing "he" to "she," or even gender-neutral words. In this paper, we focus our analysis on a popular CLM, i.e., BERT . We analyse the gender-bias it induces in five downstream tasks related to emotion and sentiment intensity prediction. For each task, we train a simple regressor utilizing BERT 's word embeddings. We then evaluate the gender-bias in regressors using an equity evaluation corpus. Ideally and from the specific design, the models should discard gender informative features from the input. However, the results show a significant dependence of the system's predictions on gender-particular words and phrases. We claim that such biases can be reduced by removing gender-specific features from word embedding. Hence, for each layer in BERT, we identify directions that primarily encode gender information. The space formed by such directions is referred to as the gender subspace in the semantic space of word embeddings. We propose an algorithm that finds fine-grained gender directions, i.e., one primary direction for each BERT layer. This obviates the need of realizing gender subspace in multiple dimensions and prevents other crucial information from being omitted. Experiments show that removing embedding components in such directions achieves great success in reducing BERT-induced bias in the downstream tasks.

article: In the contemporary big data realm, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are evolving towards more complex architectures to achieve higher inference accuracy. Model compression techniques can be leveraged to efficiently deploy such compute-intensive architectures on resource-limited mobile devices. Such methods comprise various hyperparameters that require per-layer customization to ensure high accuracy. Choosing such hyperparameters is cumbersome as the pertinent search space grows exponentially with model layers. This paper introduces GeneCAI, a novel optimization method that automatically learn s how to tune per-layer compression hyperparameters. We devise a bijective translation scheme that encodes compressed DNNs to the genotype space. Each genotype's optimality is measured using a multi-objective score based on accuracy and number of floating point operations. We develop customized genetic operations to iteratively evolve the non-dominated solutions towards the optimal Pareto front, thus, capturing the optimal trade-off between model accuracy and complexity. GeneCAI optimization method is highly scalable and can achieve a near-linear performance boost on distributed multi-GPU platforms. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that GeneCAI outperforms existing rule-based and reinforcement learning methods in DNN compression by finding models that lie on a better accuracycomplexity Pareto curve.

article: " I know, " he said, " I know. But you need to keep quiet. " His face was hidden by the shadows, his white teeth which seemed too sharp and perfect, were gleaming lightly. The girl let out a muffled cry, her tear stained face crumpled in pain. She wanted to see his face, she needed to see his face. And even if it weren't obscured by shadows she was sure that if she could see it she would go crazy. Her red ringed eyes, bloodshot and puffy, stood out bulging from their sockets. She let out a lungful of air through her nose, because her mouth was stuffed, and bloody snot flowed down her mouth and chin. She cried out again, the sounds caught behind the rag, oily and dirty, that was stuffed with great force into her mouth. Each breath was getting harder to come by now, her nose plugging up with blood and mucous. She tried to calm herself, she was sure that she was going to die and so this was not an easy task. He said again, " you need to keep quiet, " his voice was soft, low, and without any urgency. " You don't want to wake mother do you? " His face was still cloaked in the shadows but his teeth still seemed to shine, reflecting light that wasn't there. The girl shook her head side to side, no, I don't want to wake mother. I don't know who she is but I'm sure, I'm positive, I don't want to wake her. " Good, " the man said. The only light was directly behind his head, a bare bulb hanging from the ceiling. It illuminated this cold dank cellar with its bare concrete walls, a few wet cracks in the floor that she could see, and the metal ring that was secured to the floor through which the chain that held her here was fed through. A small padlock held the chain around her ankle. By now, all her moving, straining, and twisting had rubbed the skin bare causing it to blister and bleed. It was infected; it had to be by now. She had lost all sense of time since waking up here. But in all the senseless time that she had spent down here she had pieced together how she'd ended up in this unfortunate, desolate, and terrifying situation. She remembered the party she was at. Her friend Nancy had landed that elusive job she'd dreamed of since she was a child and her parents had taken her to France. The job entailed traveling the world and writing about it, reviewing hotels, local hot spots, and everything in between. She remembered showing up to the going away party for her friend. She only had two drinks; she wanted to be alright to drive home because she had her own job to get to in the morning. Nancy's boyfriend had invited his and her friends to the shindig. That must be where this faceless man fits in to the puzzle, she thought, because she'd never seen him before. Even now she couldn't remember what his face had looked like that night. As strange as that was, but she chalked it up to the drug he had slipped her. Then...she was here. Where ever this was. This cold dark room. This cellar. " Now, " the man said, " Kelly....Kelly, Kellybobelly... " he laughed, soft, crazily Kelly would say. " Now, don't even say again that this hurts. I can make it hurt a whole hell of a lot more than this...and I think you know that. Don't you? " Kelly just stared up at the black empty face, at the preternaturally glowing teeth. They looked so sharp. Yes, she thought, it could hurt a lot more. " Well then, " he said. " Let's get started shall we? " There was something in Kelly's mind, something deep down, that screamed out like a shrieking wraith and filled her head with an unbearable pain. She couldn't stand it anymore, she had a feeling, a premonition maybe, that this wasn't going to last much longer, that soon, very soon this sick fuck was going to tire of her and then what? You know damn well what missy, she thought fighting through the pain in her head, he's going to kill you and then stalk the streets for someone else to bring down here. Bring her down here, sneaking her past " mother ." The man leaned forward, his cold hand reaching out to touch her breast. Kelly's skin crawled at the thought of that corpse like touch. She spat the rag out, working her jaw to get it up and out of the back of her throat. The rag hit the floor with a wet thud. The man looked down, the teeth disappearing in a scowl. He opened his mouth to say something, but Kelly decided to show him her teeth. Kelly leaned forward and sank her teeth to the gums in his cold clammy thigh. Blood pooled readily around her mouth and she clamped her throat shut disgusted at the thought of even swallowing a drop. The man let out a startled and pained cry. " You bitch! " he yelled. Kelly groped a hand through the darkness and up his thigh. She found what she was looking for in the sweaty area between his legs and she twisted and she squeezed and she dug her nails into the hairy flesh as hard as she could and she could feel blood and maybe what is kept in those tender little plums, run down her hand. The man shrieked in pain, screaming about the mother he was apparently so worried about waking. Kelly's teeth found him again and again and again, finally finding his jugular. The blood was salty, coppery, and it pooled all around her now flowing in a great river from the wound. Kelly searched in the dim light coming from the bulb for the key that would grant her her freedom. After a long nervous moment she found it in the back pocket of shorts that the man had discarded when he walked in. She unlocked herself from her chain, stood on wobbly legs and raced as fast as those numb legs would take her for the door to the cellar. She came up the stairs that led to the cellar and found herself in a dark, damp, mouldy smelling house. All the curtains had been drawn. There was a reading room between her and the front door. In it was a leather chair enshrouded in shadows. A figure sat in the chair. She could tell this even in the darkness. Kelly moved slowly, her heart in her throat. It's mother, she thought. She shuffled her feet; the old hardwood floor creaked softly under her weight. Dust gathered between her toes. She got closer to the chair and the smell hit her like a kick in the chest. Mother was nothing more than a bloated decaying sack of flesh splitting at the seams. Kelly started to scream. She ran to the door, the sunlight hitting her for the first time in what felt like forever. And she ran, bloody and mostly naked, she ran and ran and ran.

article: They dug the trenches because the trenches help them to not get shot while they are approaching the enemy. They can dig closer and closer without getting killed. The trenches aren't just long straight ditches that nobody can get into. In the rear, they would have ramps or similar way of getting into them. The trick to trenches is to not ever leave a line of fire for a machine gun or sniper to open up on.," Here's a diagram that shows what the trench system would like like from above] (URL0) The trenches leading off the bottom part of the image would either go back to a marshaling area where new troops would enter the trench system out of range of enemy fire or else back to another set of defenses like this which would have been used if the enemy managed to take the front lines.,There was a lull starting in November 1914the German attack had been stopped, both sides were pretty much out of ammunition, and the Germans decided to defend in the West and shift troops to Russia, while the Allies decided to gather their strength for attacks the next year. That lull is when both sides dug their trenches.', "If your army has to hold a line of defense from here to there, and you know the enemy army is coming towards you, the first thing you do is look for walls and buildings to hide behind. In open areas, you start digging. Digging gives you a hole to hide in and a wall of dirt to hide behind. When you are in a long line of soldiers who are all digging you connect the holes to form a trench. What happened in WW1, was that the enemy soldiers encountered the line of trenches and stopped. Sometimes they could go around or find another road. Other times, they couldn't go around, so they dug their own trenches. The Generals on both sides of the war in France really, really didn't want this to happen. They kept trying to get around the other side's trenches. But their armies kept getting stopped by the enemy and having to dig in. Eventually, there was a solid line of trenches all the way across France, from the English Channel to Switzerland, and no way to go around.

article: Pretty simple, really. George Lucas is an extraordinary man, and his contributions to cinema are pretty much undeniable. That being said, the OT trilogy is not, or it rather shouldn't be. For one very simple reason: Lucas is an idea man. As evidenced by the prequel trilogy, he has some ideas ranging from decent to outright fantastic, but the execution was utterly dreadful. The OT trilogy, Lucas surrounded himself with talent, from screenwriters to the people who would later found Industrial Light and Magic. Back in the late 70s and 80s he had people outright push back against any idea that was awful and thus the OT trilogy came out better for it. He didn't write the script as he didn't think he was good (as he HIMSELF ADMITTED!!!) He had influence, but only when they thought the idea was genuinely good. That's the reason we got the pop culture phenomena we know today. Why Vader is so iconic. It was a collaboration of efforts, not George Lucas, who, at the end of the day got told "no" when needed. Then the Prequels happen. Why are they so garbage? Lucas surrounds himself with sycophantic yes-men. I mean he's the "great" Lucas after all, how do you say no to him? His success caused him to get a big head and no one in the crew had the balls to tell him "Okay, I think this Jar-Jar character is a really REALLY bad idea. Here's reasons why and here's how we can changefix it." So, no. George Lucas deserves some credit for OT trilogy seeing as how it was a lot of his ideas, but to the point where he's considered the father of Star Wars? No. The vast majority of what made Star Wars so good was directly because of others in the production crew telling him "Fuck no, we aren't doing that." CMV!
